words.group: Word building: -ation, -acy and -ment
words.childMeaning: A gradual gathering of something into a larger amount.
practiceSentences: An accumulation of small savings paid for the whole journey.
What accumulation of evidence changed her mind?
History is an accumulation of ordinary days as well as famous ones.
The accumulation of dust on the trunk showed how long it had stood there.
Accumulation is slow, which is why it goes unnoticed.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -acy and -ment
words.childMeaning: The quality of being correct and free from mistakes.
practiceSentences: The accuracy of the family record surprised the archivist.
How would you test the accuracy of this account?
Accuracy matters more than fluency in a translation.
She checked the dates twice for accuracy.
Accuracy is being right; precision is being exact.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -acy and -ment
words.childMeaning: The people who manage and organise a school, business, or other organisation.
practiceSentences: Why did the administration announce the cancellation so suddenly?
The administration met to discuss safety before the storm arrived.
Please listen carefully, everyone, the administration has an important announcement!
Imani passed the administration's message on to the whole class.
Administration is the running of a thing, and also the people who run it.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -acy and -ment
words.childMeaning: Movement forward, in a career or in knowledge.
practiceSentences: Her advancement to head of the archive took eleven years.
What advancement did the century bring to ordinary families?
Advancement is not the same as change.
The advancement of medicine altered how long a life lasts.
Advancement suggests a direction; progress suggests a value.

words.group: Words: family, identity and the past
words.childMeaning: A poem or song that tells a story, often handed down.
practiceSentences: The ballad carried the family's history for four generations.
How old is this ballad thought to be?
A ballad tells a story in verses and usually a refrain.
Jamal set the old ballad to a new tune.
A ballad survives because it is easy to remember.

words.group: Words: family, identity and the past
words.childMeaning: A short invented story that carries a lesson, often with animals.
practiceSentences: The fable ends with the moral stated outright.
What lesson does this fable actually teach?
A fable uses animals so nobody has to be blamed.
She wrote a fable about a river that stopped listening.
A fable admits it is invented; an anecdote does not.

words.group: Words: family, identity and the past
words.childMeaning: The pattern of qualities that makes a person who they are.
practiceSentences: Her personality comes through in every letter she wrote.
How much of a personality is formed by early years?
Personality is what stays constant across very different rooms.
The twins shared a face and almost nothing of their personality.
Personality is how you are; character is how you act.

words.group: Grammar: what a word points back to
words.childMeaning: The word that a later pronoun refers back to.
practiceSentences: In that sentence the antecedent of "they" is unclear.
Which noun is the antecedent here?
A pronoun with no clear antecedent stops a reader dead.
She rewrote the paragraph to fix a missing antecedent.
An antecedent usually comes before, which is what the word means.

words.group: Grammar: what a word points back to
words.childMeaning: A helping verb used with a main verb.
practiceSentences: In "she has finished", the auxiliary is "has".
Which auxiliary would make this a question?
An auxiliary carries the tense so the main verb need not.
English builds most of its tenses out of auxiliaries.
An auxiliary helps; the main verb does the meaning.

words.group: Grammar: what a word points back to
words.childMeaning: Depending on something else being true or happening first, often shown with 'if'.
practiceSentences: A conditional clause tells the reader exactly what must happen first.
Did you notice the conditional sentence hidden in the second paragraph?
"Every conditional sentence needs two matching halves," the teacher explained.
I realised that a conditional sentence can change the whole meaning of a promise.
A conditional makes a claim depend on something else being true.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: Continuing to work hard even when things are difficult or take a long time.
practiceSentences: Perseverance carried the research team through years of failed experiments before their breakthrough arrived.
How does perseverance differ from stubbornness when a project keeps failing?
"Perseverance beats brilliance," said the entrepreneur, "because brilliance gives up when things get boring."
It was sheer perseverance, not luck, that finally helped me master my multiplication tables years ago.
Learning an instrument rewards perseverance more than talent.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: An unfair opinion formed before you know the facts.
practiceSentences: Prejudice judges a person before meeting them.
How does the story challenge the villagers' prejudice?
She set her prejudice aside and listened properly.
Prejudice grows in the absence of real acquaintance.
The fable's lesson is that prejudice makes fools of us.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: The ability to recover quickly from difficulties or challenges.
practiceSentences: The community showed remarkable resilience by rebuilding the festival grounds within a week of the flood.
Where does a family find the resilience to celebrate joyfully during a difficult year?
"Our resilience is itself worth celebrating," declared the mayor as the repaired hall reopened.
I think resilience grows quietly through small setbacks, then reveals itself when it truly matters.
It took resilience, diligence, and the courage to lead quietly.

words.group: Words: character, feeling and growing up
words.childMeaning: A fixed, over-simple idea about a whole group of people.
practiceSentences: The story sets out to break a stereotype.
Which stereotype does this character disprove?
A stereotype ignores everything that makes a person themselves.
She refused to fit the stereotype anyone expected.
One example is never enough to justify a stereotype.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: A story whose characters and events stand for something larger.
practiceSentences: The fable is an allegory about greed.
What is this allegory really describing?
An allegory works on two levels at once.
Every character in the allegory stands for a kind of person.
An allegory says one thing and means another, on purpose.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: A way of explaining something by comparing it to something else that is similar.
practiceSentences: The coach drew an analogy between a relay team and a chain with one weak link.
Can you think of an analogy that explains why warming up matters before a sprint?
"Here is a useful analogy," said Teacher Yasmin. "Training is like saving money; small deposits grow."
I remember difficult ideas best when the teacher explains them through a vivid analogy.
The water-pipe analogy made electric current easy to picture.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: An image or idea that returns again and again in a story.
practiceSentences: Water is the central motif of the whole collection.
Which motif appears in every chapter?
A motif gathers meaning each time it returns.
The broken clock is a motif, not a coincidence.
Amara traced one motif through all four fables.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: A hint early in a story about what will happen later.
practiceSentences: The storm on page one is foreshadowing.
Where does the foreshadowing begin?
Foreshadowing makes an ending feel earned rather than sudden.
You often notice the foreshadowing only on a second reading.
Good foreshadowing hints without giving anything away.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: The order in which events actually happened.
practiceSentences: The chronology of the tale is not the order it is told in.
What chronology do these events really follow?
She drew a chronology of the whole year on one page.
A recount follows chronology; a mystery often does not.
Chronology and plot are two different things.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: A short summary that tells the main events of a story.
practiceSentences: Her synopsis left out the ending, so the class had to guess it.
A good synopsis tells the main events without spoiling the ending.
Can you write a synopsis of the legend in fewer than fifty words?
'Read the synopsis on the back cover before choosing a book,' suggested the librarian.
I wrote a synopsis of my favourite film for our class magazine.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: A long speech by one person, spoken alone or to others.
practiceSentences: The play opens with a monologue.
How long should a monologue be?
A monologue lets us hear a character think.
Dina wrote a monologue for the fox in the fable.
A monologue has one voice; a dialogue has two.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: A form of a language spoken in one area or by one group.
practiceSentences: Every region of the coast has its own dialect.
Which dialect is spoken in your grandmother's town?
A dialect is a way of speaking, not a mistake.
The story is written in dialect, so read it aloud.
A dialect has its own words and its own grammar.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: A writer's or speaker's choice of words.
practiceSentences: The poet's diction is plain and very exact.
How would you describe the diction of this speech?
Diction changes the mood more than the plot does.
Formal diction suits a report and not a fable.
Amara noticed the diction shift the moment the elder spoke.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: Clear and logical, so the parts follow one another.
practiceSentences: Rearranging the paragraphs made her argument far more coherent.
The residents presented a coherent plan for the park, complete with costs and a maintenance rota.
Is the council's transport strategy coherent, or do the bus and cycling policies contradict each other?
"Make your petition coherent," advised the librarian, "one clear demand supported by three reasons."
I redrafted my report twice before the argument felt coherent from first line to last.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: Stated openly and clearly, leaving nothing to be guessed.
practiceSentences: The instructions were explicit about the deadline.
Was the warning explicit or merely suggested?
An explicit rule saves an argument later.
She made her disagreement explicit rather than hinting.
Explicit is stated; implicit is understood.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: Suggested or understood without being said outright.
practiceSentences: Her smile had an implicit meaning that she was happy.
The packaging carried an implicit promise of luxury through its heavy paper and gold lettering.
What implicit messages about waste do children absorb from brightly wrapped party bags?
"There is an implicit agreement here," noted the teacher, "that every borrowed tool returns cleaned."
I realised the advert made an implicit health claim without stating anything it could be challenged on.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: Slight and not obvious, but there if you look carefully.
practiceSentences: There is a subtle difference between the two endings.
Was the change subtle enough to miss?
A subtle hint is easily overlooked on a first reading.
The fable makes its point in a subtle way.
Subtle is spelled with a b nobody says.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: Believable, because there is good reason to accept it.
practiceSentences: The witness gave a credible account of the evening.
Is that a credible explanation for the missing key?
A credible source names where its facts came from.
The excuse was not credible, and everyone knew it.
Credible means worth believing, not merely possible.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: Saying the opposite of something else, so both cannot be true.
practiceSentences: The two witnesses gave contradictory accounts.
Why are these instructions contradictory?
Contradictory evidence means somebody is mistaken.
His actions were contradictory to everything he had said.
Two contradictory rules cannot both be followed.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: Describing something kept fair and equal, without leaning too far to one side.
practiceSentences: A good teacher balanced kindness with clear expectations for behaviour.
Is it possible to keep a busy schedule balanced with enough rest?
Well balanced, Rohan, that argument considered both sides fairly!
The committee balanced the budget between sports and the library.
Discipline was balanced with help.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: Real and genuine; not fake or copied.
practiceSentences: The heritage tent served authentic recipes copied faithfully from great-grandmothers' handwritten notebooks.
How can visitors tell an authentic antique lamp from the clever copies sold nearby?
"This embroidery is authentic," confirmed the craftsman, "stitched exactly as my grandfather taught me."
I prefer one authentic tradition, honestly explained, to ten dazzling performances invented for tourists.
She said the school needed a leader who was authentic, not simply loud.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: To describe the special qualities or features of someone or something.
practiceSentences: Readers often characterise Sana as timid at first, yet her writing shows steady courage.
Journalists often characterise the designer as ruthless, yet her workers describe a generous employer.
How would you characterise the difference between style and fashion in a single sentence?
"I would characterise this fabric as forgiving," said the tailor, "it hides a beginner's uneven stitches."
Bold colours and carefully mended seams characterise my personal style, and I am proud of both.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: To suggest something without saying it directly.
practiceSentences: Her tone seemed to imply that she disagreed.
What does the last line imply about the ending?
A writer may imply far more than the words say.
Do not imply what you are willing to state.
To imply is the writer's side; to infer is the reader's.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: To work something out from the evidence you already have.
practiceSentences: From the muddy footprints we can deduce which way he went.
What can you deduce from the opening paragraph?
A reader deduces the ending long before it arrives.
She deduced the answer without being told any of it.
To deduce is to reason, not to guess.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: A careful judgement of a piece of work, saying what does and does not succeed.
practiceSentences: Her critique of the poem was fair and detailed.
What critique would you offer the writer?
A critique is not an attack, and not praise either.
He wrote a short critique of the article for the newsletter.
A useful critique names one thing to change first.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: To put thoughts into clear words.
practiceSentences: It takes practice to articulate a complicated opinion in front of strangers.
Residents met to articulate their concerns about the proposed motorway through the wetlands.
Who will articulate the young people's viewpoint at next month's council meeting?
"Articulate the problem in one sentence," the facilitator urged, "then we can search for solutions."
I practised until I could articulate our petition's aims without glancing at my notes.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: To follow something back to where it started.
practiceSentences: You can trace the motif back to the opening page.
Can you trace this saying to its original teller?
Historians trace the custom to a single village.
She traced the argument through every paragraph.
Trace the idea backwards and you find its source.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: To draw a wide conclusion from a small number of cases.
practiceSentences: It is unwise to generalise from one example.
Why do people generalise so quickly?
A fable invites you to generalise from one animal to many.
She refused to generalise about a whole town.
To generalise well you need more than two cases.

words.group: Words: how a story is told
words.childMeaning: To place something in the setting that explains it.
practiceSentences: A short introduction will contextualise the letter.
How would you contextualise this fable for a younger reader?
To contextualise a fact is to say when and where it belongs.
She contextualised the quotation before analysing it.
A date and a place are often enough to contextualise a source.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ability
words.childMeaning: The act of giving out or assigning something, such as tasks or money, in a set way.
practiceSentences: The council opposed the unfair allocation of tasks.
Is the allocation of duties fair across every form?
Zara argued that the allocation gave one group far too much work.
The board promised to review the allocation before the new term.
An allocation is a decision about shares, and someone always makes it.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ability
words.childMeaning: The state of having more than one possible meaning.
practiceSentences: The ambiguity in the invitation left everyone guessing the dress code.
Where does the ambiguity in this line come from?
Ambiguity is a fault in a contract and a resource in a poem.
She removed the ambiguity by naming the date outright.
Ambiguity is not the same as vagueness: it offers two clear readings, not none.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ability
words.childMeaning: How far something can be usefully applied to a situation.
practiceSentences: The rule's applicability to festivals was never tested.
What is the applicability of this finding beyond one city?
Applicability is the question a reader asks after believing you.
They doubted the applicability of the study to a rural district.
Applicability asks where an idea works, not whether it is true.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ability
words.childMeaning: A value or description that is close to the truth but not exact.
practiceSentences: Two thousand visitors was an approximation, not a count.
How good an approximation does this estimate give?
An approximation is honest as long as it says so.
The organisers worked from an approximation and were nearly right.
An approximation is close on purpose; an error is close by accident.

words.group: Words: poetry, performance and shared celebration
words.childMeaning: A short poem expressing personal feeling, or the words of a song.
practiceSentences: The lyric holds one moment rather than telling a story.
Which lyric did the singer open the festival with?
A lyric speaks in the first person more often than not.
Kofi set his grandmother's lyric to a drum rhythm.
A lyric expresses; a ballad narrates.

words.group: Words: poetry, performance and shared celebration
words.childMeaning: Working willingly with others, or a business owned by its members.
practiceSentences: The festival is run by a cooperative of twelve families.
Was the response cooperative or merely polite?
A cooperative shares its profits among the people who made them.
Their cooperative approach finished the work in half the time.
Cooperative describes an attitude, and also a kind of company.

words.group: Words: poetry, performance and shared celebration
words.childMeaning: Clearly separate and different from others.
practiceSentences: Each region brings a distinct dish to the festival.
Are these two traditions distinct or simply differently named?
A distinct difference is one you can point to.
The drumming of the two villages is quite distinct.
Distinct means clearly separate; distinctive means clearly recognisable.

words.group: Grammar: verbs that link and words that specify
words.childMeaning: Describing a verb that links a subject to what is said about it.
practiceSentences: In "she is a dancer", the copular verb is "is".
Which copular verb would you use here?
A copular verb joins rather than acts.
Be, seem and become are the commonest copular verbs.
A copular verb takes no object; it takes a complement.

words.group: Grammar: verbs that link and words that specify
words.childMeaning: A word before a noun that shows which one or how many.
practiceSentences: "The", "this" and "every" are determiners.
Which determiner makes the meaning most specific?
A determiner narrows a noun before any adjective does.
English requires a determiner where many languages do not.
A determiner points; an adjective describes.

words.group: Grammar: verbs that link and words that specify
words.childMeaning: Describing a verb form that shows tense and agrees with its subject.
practiceSentences: In "she walks home", the finite verb is "walks".
Which verb in this clause is finite?
Every complete sentence needs at least one finite verb.
A finite verb changes with the subject; an infinitive does not.
Finite here means limited by tense and person, not merely countable.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The band of colours light splits into, or a full range of something.
practiceSentences: A prism splits white light into a spectrum.
Which colour sits at the end of the spectrum?
Astronomers read a star's spectrum to learn what it is made of.
A rainbow is a spectrum you can see from the ground.
The spectrum runs from red through to violet.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: Speed in one stated direction.
practiceSentences: The rocket must reach a huge velocity to escape Earth.
What velocity does the probe need?
Velocity is speed with a direction attached.
They measured the velocity of the falling weight.
A small change in velocity alters the whole orbit.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The process of burning, which gives out heat and light.
practiceSentences: Combustion needs fuel, heat and oxygen.
What happens to the fuel during combustion?
Combustion in the engine pushes the piston down.
Without oxygen, combustion stops at once.
The rocket rises on the force of combustion.

words.group: Words: space, matter and the universe
words.childMeaning: The study of how living things relate to each other and their surroundings.
practiceSentences: Ecology looks at the whole system, not one animal.
Why does ecology matter to farmers?
Her interest in ecology began with a rock pool.
Ecology explains why removing one species matters.
The class studied the ecology of the riverbank.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: The stage when a child's body develops into an adult's.
practiceSentences: Puberty begins at different ages for different people.
What changes happen to the body during puberty?
Puberty is driven by hormones released inside the body.
There is no single right age for puberty to start.
Puberty takes several years, not a single moment.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: A chemical messenger the body makes to control how it works.
practiceSentences: A hormone travels through the blood to reach its target.
Which hormone controls how tall a person grows?
Hormones work slowly compared with nerve signals.
One hormone can affect several parts of the body at once.
The class labelled where each hormone is made.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: A substance in food that the body needs to live and grow.
practiceSentences: Beans are a good source of every main nutrient.
Which nutrient does the body use for building muscle?
A nutrient the body cannot make must come from food.
Cooking for too long destroys some of the nutrients.
Water carries nutrients to every cell.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: A nutrient the body needs in small amounts to stay healthy.
practiceSentences: Oranges are rich in vitamin C.
Which vitamin does sunlight help the body make?
A vitamin is needed in tiny amounts, but needed all the same.
Vitamins are lost when vegetables are boiled too long.
No single vitamin can replace a varied diet.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: A protein the body makes to attack a particular germ.
practiceSentences: The body makes an antibody shaped to fit one germ.
How long does an antibody stay in the blood?
An antibody remembers a germ it has met before.
A vaccine teaches the body to make the antibody early.
Each antibody works on one invader and no other.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: The removal of waste the body has produced.
practiceSentences: Excretion removes what the body cannot use.
Which organs are involved in excretion?
Excretion and digestion are not the same process.
Sweating is a form of excretion as well as cooling.
Without excretion, waste would build up and poison the body.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: The process by which living things produce young.
practiceSentences: Reproduction is one of the signs of a living thing.
How does reproduction differ between plants and animals?
Reproduction passes characteristics from parent to offspring.
Some plants manage reproduction without any seeds.
Reproduction also means making a copy of a picture.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: A substance that speeds up a chemical change inside the body.
practiceSentences: An enzyme in saliva begins breaking down starch.
Which enzyme acts on protein in the stomach?
An enzyme speeds a reaction without being used up.
Enzymes stop working if they get too hot.
Each enzyme fits one job, like a key in a lock.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: The joining of a male and a female cell to begin new life.
practiceSentences: Fertilisation is the first step in reproduction.
Where does fertilisation take place in a flower?
After fertilisation the cell begins to divide.
Fertilisation in fish usually happens in the water.
Fertilisation also describes feeding soil for crops.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: A living thing at the earliest stage of its growth.
practiceSentences: The embryo grows from a single fertilised cell.
How long does the embryo stage last?
An embryo is protected inside the seed or the body.
The embryo of a bean sits between the two halves.
Every large animal began as an embryo too small to see.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: How quickly something's speed is changing.
practiceSentences: A sprinter's acceleration matters more than her top speed.
What causes the acceleration at the start of a race?
Acceleration is a change in speed, not speed itself.
The car's acceleration was measured over ten metres.
Slowing down is acceleration too, in the opposite direction.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: To do with movement, or the energy a moving thing has.
practiceSentences: A moving ball carries kinetic energy.
How much kinetic energy does a runner have?
Kinetic energy grows quickly as speed increases.
A stretched bow stores energy and releases it as kinetic.
Kinetic comes from the Greek word for motion.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: A force that slows something down as it moves through air or water.
practiceSentences: A swimmer's cap reduces resistance in the water.
How does a cyclist lower air resistance?
Resistance grows as a moving object goes faster.
The parachute works by creating as much resistance as possible.
Resistance in a wire turns electrical energy into heat.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: To move something from one place, person or form to another.
practiceSentences: Energy transfers from the muscles to the ball.
How does heat transfer through a metal spoon?
The player asked for a transfer to another club.
Transfer the reading into the table before you leave.
Energy is never lost, only transferred.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Dealing with something difficult without being overwhelmed.
practiceSentences: Coping with a loss takes longer than people expect.
What coping strategies help before a big match?
Coping is not the same as pretending nothing is wrong.
She has her own way of coping with a noisy house.
Asking for help is a form of coping, not a failure of it.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Making yourself do what you planned, even when you would rather not.
practiceSentences: Training every morning takes real self-discipline.
Where does self-discipline come from?
Self-discipline is a habit long before it is a feeling.
Amal's self-discipline showed in her steady improvement.
Self-discipline is choosing later over now.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Knowing about or understanding something.
practiceSentences: The campaign raised awareness of safe cycling.
What awareness does a goalkeeper need of the whole pitch?
Awareness of a risk is the first step to avoiding it.
Her awareness of the rules saved the team a penalty.
Awareness is noticing; action is what follows.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Understanding your own feelings, strengths and limits.
practiceSentences: Self-awareness helps an athlete know when to rest.
How would you describe your own self-awareness?
Self-awareness means noticing a mood before it becomes a mistake.
Dina showed self-awareness by admitting she had rushed.
Self-awareness is harder than being aware of everybody else.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: The ability to change to suit new conditions.
practiceSentences: Adaptability matters more than strength on a changing pitch.
What adaptability does a new sport demand?
Adaptability is a skill that can be practised.
The team's adaptability won them the second half.
Adaptability is not the same as having no plan.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Belonging is the comfortable feeling of being accepted and welcome as part of a group.
practiceSentences: Sami felt a sense of belonging the moment he stepped into the square.
Why does belonging matter so much during a community celebration?
Nora described a deep sense of belonging whenever the drummers began to play!
The shared feast created a feeling of belonging that lasted long after the festival ended.
What they all share is a sense of joy, belonging, and gratitude.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Involving a great deal of effort in a short time.
practiceSentences: The squad began an intensive week of training.
Is intensive practice better than steady practice?
An intensive course covers a term in a fortnight.
Intensive training without rest causes injury.
Intensive means concentrated, not merely long.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Continuing steadily even when it is difficult.
practiceSentences: A persistent cough should be shown to a doctor.
Was she persistent or simply stubborn?
Persistent effort beats occasional brilliance.
The persistent rain cancelled every fixture.
Persistent means it keeps going, whether you want it to or not.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Able to be easily hurt or harmed, either physically or emotionally.
practiceSentences: City planners must protect vulnerable pedestrians, especially children and elderly residents, at busy crossings.
Which neighbourhoods are most vulnerable to flooding, and how should the council respond first?
"Cyclists feel vulnerable on this roundabout," reported Rohan, presenting the survey results to the council.
I never realised how vulnerable pedestrians felt on our street until I pushed my brother's wheelchair.
She felt vulnerable, like a balloon drifting away without string.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Able to change easily to suit a new situation.
practiceSentences: An adaptable player can cover two positions.
How adaptable is this training plan?
Adaptable equipment suits players of every size.
The coach wanted an adaptable squad, not eleven specialists.
Adaptable describes the person; adaptability is the quality.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Not as much as is needed.
practiceSentences: Insufficient sleep slows every kind of recovery.
Was the warm-up insufficient for such a cold day?
Insufficient evidence is not the same as evidence against.
One bottle of water proved insufficient for the whole team.
Insufficient means short of enough, not close to nothing.

words.group: Words: the body, movement and health
words.childMeaning: Good enough to be allowed or agreed to.
practiceSentences: A draw was an acceptable result away from home.
Is that an acceptable excuse for missing training?
An acceptable standard is a floor, not a target.
The referee ruled the boots acceptable.
What is acceptable in practice may not be in a match.

words.group: Word building: -ption, -ity and -ence
words.childMeaning: Something taken to be true without being checked.
practiceSentences: The whole plan rested on an assumption nobody had tested.
What assumption is this advertisement making about you?
An assumption is a decision you did not notice making.
She listed her assumptions before starting the calculation.
An assumption is unexamined; a premise is stated on purpose.

words.group: Word building: -ption, -ity and -ence
words.childMeaning: The state of having many parts that affect one another.
practiceSentences: The complexity of a supply chain hides where the harm happens.
How much complexity can one label usefully carry?
Complexity is not the same as difficulty.
The complexity of the dye process surprised the whole class.
Complexity is why simple answers about clothing are usually wrong.

words.group: Word building: -ption, -ity and -ence
words.childMeaning: What something is made of, or the way its parts are arranged.
practiceSentences: The label lists the composition of the fabric.
What is the composition of this blend?
Composition decides how a garment wears and how it washes.
The composition of the class photograph took twenty minutes.
Composition can mean the mixture, or the arrangement, or a piece of writing.

words.group: Word building: -ption, -ity and -ence
words.childMeaning: Behaving or happening in the same way each time.
practiceSentences: The dye lacked consistency between batches.
Is there consistency between what the brand says and what it does?
Consistency is what makes a claim testable.
Her consistency over eight months persuaded the buyer.
Consistency also describes how thick or thin a liquid is.

words.group: Words: what clothes cost the world
words.childMeaning: Grown without artificial chemicals, or to do with living things.
practiceSentences: Organic cotton is grown without synthetic pesticides.
Is organic always better for the land?
Organic farming uses more land for the same yield.
The word organic also means anything containing carbon.
Organic on a label is a legal claim, not a compliment.

words.group: Words: what clothes cost the world
words.childMeaning: A poisonous substance, especially one made by a living thing.
practiceSentences: Some dyes release a toxin into the river below the mill.
Which toxin does this process leave behind?
A toxin harms in small amounts, which is what makes it one.
Strictly, a toxin is produced by an organism; a poison need not be.
The toxin was traced to a single discharge pipe.

words.group: Words: what clothes cost the world
words.childMeaning: The amount of material or energy wasted in a process.
practiceSentences: Cutting a pattern badly increases the loss of fabric.
What loss does each stage of this process accept?
A loss of ten per cent at four stages is not a loss of ten per cent.
Heat loss makes the dryer the costliest machine in the building.
Loss also means no longer having something you valued.

words.group: Words: what clothes cost the world
words.childMeaning: An organisation of workers formed to protect their interests.
practiceSentences: The garment workers formed a union after the third wage cut.
What can a union do that one worker cannot?
A union bargains for many so that no one bargains alone.
The union negotiated a safety inspection into the contract.
Union also means the joining of two things into one.

words.group: Grammar: verb forms that change their job
words.childMeaning: The basic form of a verb, usually written with the word to in front of it, such as to run.
practiceSentences: The infinitive is the form you find in a dictionary.
Which infinitive follows this verb?
An infinitive does not change with the subject.
She split the infinitive deliberately and nobody minded.
An infinitive names the action; a finite verb places it in time.

words.group: Grammar: verb forms that change their job
words.childMeaning: A word or phrase that changes the meaning of another word.
practiceSentences: A modifier placed wrongly can attach itself to the nearest noun.
Which modifier is doing the work in this phrase?
A modifier adds detail; it does not add a new idea.
Adjectives and adverbs are the commonest modifiers.
A dangling modifier describes something the sentence never mentions.

words.group: Grammar: verb forms that change their job
words.childMeaning: A verb form, often ending in -ed or -ing, used to build other tenses or describe a noun.
practiceSentences: In "the torn label", "torn" is a past participle.
Which participle opens this sentence?
A participle can act as an adjective or help build a tense.
The present participle ends in -ing in every case.
A participle is a verb form doing a describing job.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: The ability to see what needs to be done and do it without being told.
practiceSentences: Maya showed initiative by organising a homework club before any teacher had suggested it.
Why do employers value initiative so highly when they interview school leavers?
"Use your initiative," said the manager. "If the shelf is empty, restock it without waiting to be asked."
Taking the initiative to email the museum myself led to the best work-experience week imaginable.
The recycling scheme began as one student's initiative.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Living or happening at the same time; modern.
practiceSentences: The new library blends contemporary glass architecture with the restored stonework of the old station.
Should contemporary buildings match their historic neighbours, or proudly display their own era?
"Contemporary cities must plan for climate change," argued the guest engineer at our assembly.
I admire contemporary designers who treat pavements and bus stops as seriously as skyscrapers.
The gallery pairs traditional weaving with contemporary art.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Causing strong disagreement between people.
practiceSentences: The decision proved controversial across the whole town.
Why is this rule so controversial?
A controversial topic needs careful handling.
The referee made a controversial call.
Nothing controversial was said at the meeting.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Following the usual rules or traditions.
practiceSentences: She chose a conventional opening for her essay.
Is that the conventional way to do it?
Conventional methods are not always the best.
The design is conventional but very well made.
He gave the conventional answer and moved on.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Something that saves money or uses resources wisely.
practiceSentences: Cooking one large pot of soup is far more economical than buying lunch daily.
Buses are more economical than cars because many people share one journey.
Which is more economical, buying one big bag of rice or several small ones?
'Turning off lights is an economical habit,' reminded Dad, flicking the switch.
I found an economical way to make bookmarks from old greeting cards.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Basic, and forming the foundation of something.
practiceSentences: Reading is fundamental to everything else at school.
What fundamental rule does the game rest on?
There is a fundamental difference between the two.
Fundamental skills need regular practice.
Trust is fundamental to any friendship.

words.group: Words: judging and describing carefully
words.childMeaning: Not good enough for what is needed.
practiceSentences: One blanket proved inadequate for that cold.
Was the lighting inadequate for reading?
Inadequate notes made the revision harder.
The old bridge is inadequate for heavy lorries.
An inadequate answer is worse than none at all.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: The variety of plants, animals, and other living things found in an area.
practiceSentences: Biodiversity decreases whenever a forest like this one is cleared.
Why is biodiversity so important for a healthy ecosystem, Teacher Yasmin?
This reserve has incredible biodiversity, Amal exclaimed!
Scientists measure biodiversity by counting the different species in an area.
Wetlands protect coastal towns and support rich biodiversity.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: A thread inside a cell that carries the genes.
practiceSentences: Each chromosome carries hundreds of genes.
How many chromosomes does a human cell hold?
A chromosome is only visible when a cell divides.
Half of every chromosome pair comes from each parent.
Chromosome means coloured body, from the dye that first revealed it.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: A section of a chromosome that decides one inherited feature.
practiceSentences: A gene decides whether the seed grows tall or short.
Which gene controls the colour of the coat?
One gene can be carried without ever being shown.
Genes are passed on whole, not blended.
A gene is an instruction; the animal is the result.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: The passing of features from parents to their young.
practiceSentences: Eye colour is decided by inheritance.
What features come to a cub through inheritance?
Inheritance explains why offspring resemble their parents.
Inheritance passes on the instructions, not the experiences.
Inheritance also means property left to somebody.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: The young form of an insect, quite unlike the adult.
practiceSentences: The larva looks nothing like the moth it becomes.
What does this larva eat before it pupates?
A larva must moult before it can grow further.
Mosquito larvae live in still water.
The plural of larva is larvae, not larvas.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: A living thing too small to see without a microscope.
practiceSentences: A single spoonful of soil holds millions of microorganisms.
Which microorganisms break down fallen leaves?
Not every microorganism causes disease.
Microorganisms were unknown until the lens was invented.
A microorganism can be a bacterium, a fungus or an alga.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: An animal with a backbone.
practiceSentences: A frog is a vertebrate and a beetle is not.
Which vertebrates live in this river?
Every vertebrate has an internal skeleton.
Fish were the first vertebrates to appear.
Vertebrates are a small share of all animal species.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: An animal without a backbone.
practiceSentences: Most animals on Earth are invertebrates.
Which invertebrate is the largest?
An invertebrate may still have a hard outer shell.
Worms, insects and jellyfish are all invertebrates.
Invertebrate simply means not a vertebrate.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: A living thing that breaks down dead material.
practiceSentences: Fungi are the forest's most important decomposers.
What would happen without decomposers?
A decomposer returns nutrients to the soil.
Decomposers are the last link, and also the first.
Bacteria and fungi are the two great groups of decomposers.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: Able to make food from sunlight, water and air.
practiceSentences: Photosynthetic plants sit at the base of every food chain.
Which photosynthetic organisms live in the sea?
A photosynthetic cell contains chlorophyll.
Some bacteria are photosynthetic as well as plants.
Photosynthetic describes the organism; photosynthesis is what it does.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: The control centre of a cell, holding its chromosomes.
practiceSentences: The nucleus holds the instructions for the whole cell.
Which part of the cell is the nucleus?
A cell without a nucleus cannot divide normally.
The nucleus is separated from the rest by a membrane.
Nucleus also names the centre of an atom.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: The spreading of a substance from where there is more to where there is less.
practiceSentences: Oxygen reaches the blood by diffusion.
How does diffusion move a scent across a room?
Diffusion needs no pump and no energy.
Diffusion stops when the amounts even out.
A drop of ink spreading through water is diffusion.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: Material that settles at the bottom of a liquid.
practiceSentences: Sediment settles where the river slows down.
What sediment did the flood leave behind?
Layers of sediment record thousands of years.
Sediment buries the remains that later become fossils.
Stir the bottle and the sediment lifts again.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: Something that speeds up a change without being used up itself.
practiceSentences: A catalyst speeds the reaction and survives it.
Which catalyst does this process need?
An enzyme is the body's own kind of catalyst.
Without a catalyst the change would take days.
A catalyst is also a person who makes something happen.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: A liquid that dissolves another substance.
practiceSentences: Water is the solvent in almost every living cell.
Which solvent will dissolve this stain?
A solvent does the dissolving; the solute is dissolved.
Warming the solvent makes it work faster.
Water is called the universal solvent for good reason.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: Easily broken or damaged.
practiceSentences: A coral reef is beautiful and extremely fragile.
Why is this habitat so fragile after a dry season?
A fragile ecosystem recovers slowly, if it recovers at all.
The eggs are fragile, so the rangers move nobody near them.
Fragile does not mean unimportant; it means easily lost.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: Able to continue for a long time without using everything up.
practiceSentences: Sustainable fishing leaves enough behind to breed.
Is this way of farming sustainable?
A sustainable harvest takes the interest, not the capital.
The reserve was designed to be sustainable for a century.
Sustainable asks what happens in fifty years, not next season.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: Always changing or full of energy and movement.
practiceSentences: A river delta is a dynamic landscape.
How dynamic is this population from year to year?
A dynamic system settles into no single state.
The herd's dynamic movement follows the rain.
Dynamic is the opposite of static.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: Affecting or covering the whole world.
practiceSentences: Migration routes are a global phenomenon.
What global change threatens this species?
A global problem needs more than a local answer.
The survey collected global data over ten years.
Global means worldwide, not merely widespread.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: Next to or beside something else.
practiceSentences: The reserve is adjacent to the farmland.
Which habitat is adjacent to the wetland?
Two adjacent fields can hold quite different species.
Animals move between adjacent habitats through the corridor.
Adjacent means touching, or very nearly.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: Very unusual, remarkable, or far beyond what is normal.
practiceSentences: Sami showed extraordinary courage when he returned from injury.
What made that extraordinary comeback possible, do you think, Nora?
What an extraordinary finish that race turned out to be!
Teacher Yasmin called it an extraordinary achievement for such a young runner.
Ordinary people can do extraordinary things in a crisis.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: To watch something carefully over a period of time.
practiceSentences: Rangers monitor the herd throughout the dry season.
How often should we monitor the water level?
To monitor is to watch over time, not to glance once.
Amal monitors the nest from a distance so the birds settle.
A monitor is also the screen the readings appear on.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: To measure something and express it as a number.
practiceSentences: It is hard to quantify the damage after one season.
How would you quantify the size of this population?
To quantify a change you need a measurement from before.
They quantified the loss in hectares rather than in words.
Some things matter and cannot be quantified.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: To see or show how two things are not the same.
practiceSentences: Can you differentiate a crocodile from an alligator?
How do you differentiate these two footprints?
Size alone will not differentiate the male from the female.
She learned to differentiate the calls by ear.
To differentiate is to name the difference, not just feel it.

words.group: Words: living things and how they pass life on
words.childMeaning: To examine something very closely and carefully.
practiceSentences: Scrutinise the photograph before naming the species.
Why scrutinise a result you already expected?
A scientist must scrutinise the method as well as the answer.
They scrutinised every entry in the field notebook.
To scrutinise is to look harder than seems necessary.

words.group: Word building: -tion, -ity and -ation
words.childMeaning: The building of something, or the way it is put together.
practiceSentences: Construction of the ring road took four years.
What construction method suits soft ground?
Construction is the noisiest promise a city ever makes.
The bridge's construction used far less steel than expected.
Construction can mean the building, the process, or the arrangement of a sentence.

words.group: Word building: -tion, -ity and -ation
words.childMeaning: The ability to use imagination to make or think of new and original things.
practiceSentences: The bus shelter design showed real creativity within a tiny budget.
What sparks your creativity most, a strange image or an unusual sound?
Creativity in planning is usually a constraint met well.
Zara's proposal proved that creativity can come from the smallest, quietest ideas.
Certainly, the energy and creativity of young East Africans are making a difference.

words.group: Word building: -tion, -ity and -ation
words.childMeaning: The quality of deserving to be believed.
practiceSentences: The council lost credibility when the third deadline passed.
What gives this report its credibility?
Credibility is slow to build and quick to spend.
Publishing the raw figures restored some credibility.
Credibility is about the source; plausibility is about the claim.

words.group: Word building: -tion, -ity and -ation
words.childMeaning: The act of telling or making things different from one another.
practiceSentences: Differentiation between the two routes matters at rush hour.
What differentiation does this map actually show?
Differentiation begins with noticing that a difference exists.
The survey used colour for differentiation between districts.
Differentiation also names a method in mathematics.

words.group: Words: cities, government and who they serve
words.childMeaning: An unfair difference in what people have or can get.
practiceSentences: Inequality shows in how long a journey to work takes.
What inequality does this map make visible?
Inequality is a difference that somebody could have prevented.
The report measured inequality between districts of the same city.
In mathematics an inequality is something else entirely: a statement that two amounts differ.

words.group: Words: cities, government and who they serve
words.childMeaning: To change something slightly to make it better or more suitable.
practiceSentences: They modified the junction rather than rebuilding it.
How would you modify this design for a narrower street?
To modify is to adjust what exists, not to replace it.
The plan was modified three times before approval.
In grammar, a word that modifies another changes its meaning.

words.group: Grammar: the part that says something about the subject
words.childMeaning: The part of a sentence that says something about the subject.
practiceSentences: In "the bus arrived late", the predicate is "arrived late".
Which words form the predicate here?
A predicate always contains a verb.
She split each sentence into subject and predicate.
The subject names it; the predicate says what about it.

words.group: Grammar: the part that says something about the subject
words.childMeaning: A word that tells you how much or how many.
practiceSentences: "Many", "few" and "several" are quantifiers.
Which quantifier fits an uncountable noun?
A quantifier answers how much before anything is described.
English uses different quantifiers for countable and uncountable nouns.
A quantifier counts; a determiner points.

words.group: Grammar: the part that says something about the subject
words.childMeaning: A verb form used for wishes, suggestions and unreal situations.
practiceSentences: In "if I were you", the subjunctive is "were".
Where would a subjunctive be used in this sentence?
The subjunctive survives in English mostly in set phrases.
She used the subjunctive and it sounded unexpectedly formal.
The subjunctive describes what is wished for, not what is.

words.group: Words: how a story is built
words.childMeaning: The character who stands against the main character.
practiceSentences: The antagonist blocks whatever the hero wants.
Who is the antagonist in this legend?
A good antagonist believes they are right.
The antagonist need not be a person at all.
Hunger itself is the antagonist of that tale.

words.group: Words: how a story is built
words.childMeaning: The way a writer shows what a character is like.
practiceSentences: Her characterisation is done through small actions.
What characterisation do the first two pages give us?
Good characterisation shows rather than tells.
The characterisation of the trickster is the tale's best part.
Dialogue is a tool of characterisation.

words.group: Words: how a story is built
words.childMeaning: Using an object or image to stand for a bigger idea.
practiceSentences: The symbolism of the broken pot is clear by the end.
What symbolism does the river carry here?
Symbolism lets a story say two things at once.
A dove is the oldest symbolism for peace.
Not every object is symbolism; sometimes a pot is a pot.

words.group: Words: how a story is built
words.childMeaning: When what happens is the opposite of what was expected.
practiceSentences: The irony is that the map led them home.
Where is the irony in this ending?
Irony can be gentle or bitter.
There is irony in a fire station burning down.
The reader sees the irony before the character does.

words.group: Words: how a story is built
words.childMeaning: Deliberate exaggeration used for effect.
practiceSentences: "I have told you a million times" is hyperbole.
Which line is hyperbole rather than fact?
Hyperbole is not lying; nobody is meant to believe it.
The tale uses hyperbole to make the giant enormous.
A little hyperbole is funny; a lot is tiring.

words.group: Words: how a story is built
words.childMeaning: Felt or done by two people towards each other.
practiceSentences: Their respect was mutual from the start.
Is the agreement mutual, or one-sided?
They found a mutual friend at the market.
Mutual trust took years to build.
The decision was mutual, so neither resented it.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: A way of writing numbers using only 0 and 1.
practiceSentences: A computer stores everything as binary.
What is the number five in binary?
Binary uses two digits where we use ten.
Each binary digit is called a bit.
Binary is a choice between two states, on or off.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: Writing the instructions that tell a computer what to do.
practiceSentences: Coding is a way of thinking before it is a way of typing.
What language did you start coding in?
Coding rewards somebody who enjoys being wrong quickly.
The club meets on Thursdays for coding.
Coding is the writing; the program is the result.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: Finding and fixing the mistakes in a program.
practiceSentences: Debugging takes longer than writing the code did.
Where would you start debugging this?
Debugging is easier if you change one thing at a time.
She spent the whole afternoon debugging a single line.
The word debugging comes from a real moth in a real machine.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: The design and building of machines that can act on their own.
practiceSentences: Robotics brings together coding, electronics and engineering.
What can robotics do that a person cannot?
Robotics needs a sensor as much as it needs a motor.
The robotics club built an arm that sorts by colour.
Robotics is a field; a robot is one thing in it.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: A model that copies how something real behaves, so it can be studied.
practiceSentences: A simulation lets you crash the bridge without building it.
How accurate is this simulation?
A simulation is only as good as what was put into it.
Pilots train on a simulation before they fly.
A simulation predicts; it does not prove.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: Running or controlling something, as an operating system runs a computer.
practiceSentences: The operating system starts before anything else does.
Which operating system does this machine use?
An operating system shares the processor between programs.
She was operating the machine when it stopped.
An operating system is the program every other program stands on.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: Software stored permanently inside a device.
practiceSentences: The printer's firmware controls how it feeds paper.
When was the firmware last updated?
Firmware sits between hardware and ordinary software.
A firmware update can add features to a device you already own.
Firmware is firm because it is not meant to change often.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: A device connected to a computer to add to what it can do.
practiceSentences: A mouse is a peripheral, not part of the computer itself.
Which peripheral would help most here?
A peripheral can be added or removed without opening the case.
The scanner is the only peripheral the room shares.
Peripheral also means at the edge, and that is the same idea.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: An agreed set of rules for how two machines exchange information.
practiceSentences: Two machines can only talk if they share a protocol.
Which protocol does this connection use?
A protocol settles the order and the format in advance.
The web runs on a protocol agreed decades ago.
A protocol is also the correct way to behave on a formal occasion.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: Connecting computers so they can share information.
practiceSentences: Networking lets one printer serve a whole room.
What networking does the school building need?
Networking turns many machines into one shared resource.
A networking fault can look exactly like a broken program.
Networking also means building useful contacts among people.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: A store of recently used data, kept close by so it can be fetched fast.
practiceSentences: The browser keeps a cache so the page loads faster next time.
Why does clearing the cache sometimes fix a page?
A cache trades a little memory for a lot of speed.
A stale cache shows you yesterday's version of a page.
Cache is pronounced like cash, not like cachet.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: The mark on a screen showing where the next action will happen.
practiceSentences: The cursor blinks where the next letter will appear.
Where is the cursor now?
A cursor changes shape to say what a click will do.
She moved the cursor to the end of the line.
The cursor was named after a sliding part of a slide rule.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: Running inside a web browser rather than installed on the machine.
practiceSentences: The whole tool is browser-based, so nothing is installed.
Is this browser-based or does it need downloading?
A browser-based program updates for everyone at once.
Browser-based tools work on any machine with a browser.
Browser-based means the browser is doing the running.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: Stored and run on distant servers rather than on your own device.
practiceSentences: Their cloud-based storage keeps a copy off the premises.
Is a cloud-based system safer than a local one?
A cloud-based service works from any device you sign in on.
Cloud-based files survive a broken laptop.
Cloud-based means somebody else's computer, somewhere else.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: To think out and plan something new.
practiceSentences: They set out to devise a cheaper way to pump water.
How would you devise a test for this?
To devise is to invent the method, not just the idea.
She devised a system that needed no electricity.
Devise is the verb; a device is what it produces.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: To find out what is going wrong and put it right.
practiceSentences: Troubleshoot the power supply before blaming the software.
How would you troubleshoot a machine that will not start?
To troubleshoot is to work from the simplest cause upwards.
She troubleshoots by removing one part at a time.
Troubleshooting is a method, not a talent.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: To improve something by small, careful changes.
practiceSentences: Each version of the prototype refined the last.
What would you refine before showing it to anyone?
To refine is to improve by small steps, not to start again.
They refined the design over eleven attempts.
Refining is where most of the invention actually happens.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: To include something as part of a larger whole.
practiceSentences: The architects promised to incorporate green roofs and rain gardens into the new sports hall design.
Should the geography syllabus incorporate a yearly field trip to the wetland reserve?
"Try to incorporate your survey data into the poster," said the teacher, "so your argument has evidence."
I decided to incorporate a section on renewable energy into my presentation about protecting the coast.
The final design will incorporate ideas from every year group.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: To handle or work something skilfully, especially with the hands or with data.
practiceSentences: The robot arm can manipulate objects too small for fingers.
How does the program manipulate the data?
Long tongs let you manipulate something far too hot to touch.
She manipulated the figures into a chart in one step.
Manipulate can also mean to control a person unfairly, which is a different thing entirely.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: To make practical use of something.
practiceSentences: The design utilises heat that would otherwise be wasted.
What materials could we utilise instead?
To utilise is to put to use, often something already there.
They utilised old bicycle parts in the frame.
Utilise usually means use, and use is usually the better word.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: To change something slightly so it fits.
practiceSentences: Adjust the strap until the frame sits level.
What would you adjust first?
Adjust one thing at a time or you will not know what helped.
He adjusted the timing and the motor ran smoothly.
To adjust is to change a little; to redesign is to start again.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: To begin, especially something formal or planned.
practiceSentences: Building will commence once the drawings are approved.
When does the competition commence?
Work commenced before the materials arrived, which was a mistake.
The ceremony commenced at exactly nine o'clock.
Commence is the formal word; begin does the same work.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: New in a way that improves on what came before.
practiceSentences: The cooling design was genuinely innovative.
What makes an idea innovative rather than merely new?
An innovative solution often looks obvious afterwards.
Their innovative use of clay kept the water cold.
Innovative means it works AND it is new; new alone is not enough.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: Possible to actually do.
practiceSentences: The plan is feasible if the parts arrive on time.
Is a solar version feasible for a village?
Feasible asks whether it CAN be done, not whether it should be.
They rejected two designs and kept the feasible one.
A feasible idea is one you could start on Monday.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: To do with the practical details of how something works.
practiceSentences: The technical drawing shows every measurement.
What technical problem stopped the first model?
A technical explanation is not the same as a clear one.
She read the technical manual twice before starting.
Technical detail belongs in an appendix, not an introduction.

words.group: Words: building, coding and making things work
words.childMeaning: A different choice or option.
practiceSentences: When rain flooded the pitch, the coaches quickly arranged an alternative venue in the sports hall.
Is there a realistic alternative to expensive new stadiums for cities that host the Games?
"Swimming is an excellent alternative," the physiotherapist said, "while your ankle finishes healing."
I chose badminton as my alternative activity this term, and now I secretly prefer it to football.
Cycling offers a cheap alternative to the crowded buses.

words.group: Word building: -ery, -ness and -ility
words.childMeaning: The finding of something that was not known before.
practiceSentences: The discovery of the nesting site changed the whole survey.
What discovery would settle this question?
A discovery is only the beginning of the work.
Her discovery was published two years after she made it.
A discovery finds what existed; an invention makes what did not.

words.group: Word building: -ery, -ness and -ility
words.childMeaning: How well something achieves what it was meant to.
practiceSentences: The effectiveness of the fence was measured over three seasons.
How would you test the effectiveness of this method?
Effectiveness asks whether it worked, not whether it was cheap.
The scheme's effectiveness fell once the funding ended.
Effectiveness is doing the right thing; efficiency is doing it with less.

words.group: Word building: -ery, -ness and -ility
words.childMeaning: The ability to change easily to suit new conditions.
practiceSentences: A plan needs flexibility when the weather decides the timetable.
What flexibility does this route allow?
Flexibility costs something: a flexible plan is rarely the cheapest.
The team's flexibility saved the expedition on day four.
Flexibility bends; fragility breaks.

words.group: Word building: -ery, -ness and -ility
words.childMeaning: A broad conclusion drawn from particular cases.
practiceSentences: One dry season is not enough for a generalisation.
What generalisation does this data actually support?
A generalisation is useful until it meets the case it cannot hold.
She avoided a generalisation and reported what she saw.
A generalisation reaches beyond the evidence, which is its purpose and its risk.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: Describing gases that trap heat in the Earth's atmosphere.
practiceSentences: Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
How does the greenhouse effect keep the planet liveable?
The greenhouse effect is natural; its strengthening is not.
Greenhouse gases let sunlight in and slow the heat leaving.
A greenhouse is also a glass building, which is where the comparison comes from.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: A compound containing two oxygen atoms joined to another element.
practiceSentences: Carbon dioxide holds one carbon atom and two of oxygen.
Which dioxide is produced when sulphur burns?
The di in dioxide means two, as it does in dialogue.
Sulphur dioxide from the works turned the rain acidic.
A dioxide has two oxygens; a monoxide has one.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: The process by which some living things survive to breed and others do not.
practiceSentences: Natural selection acts on variation that already exists.
What pressure is driving selection on this island?
Selection does not plan; it only keeps what survives.
Over generations, selection made the beaks measurably deeper.
Selection also means simply choosing, which is what makes the term easy to misread.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: To say what is likely to happen, using what is known now.
practiceSentences: They forecast the rains three weeks early and were right.
What does the model forecast for the next decade?
To forecast is to be precise about uncertainty.
The forecast was wrong, which is not the same as careless.
A forecast states a probability; a prediction often pretends not to.

words.group: Grammar: verbs that take an object, and verbs that do not
words.childMeaning: Describing a verb that takes an object.
practiceSentences: In "she carried the pack", "carried" is transitive.
Which verb in this sentence is transitive?
A transitive verb needs something to act on.
Many verbs are transitive in one sentence and not in the next.
A transitive verb takes an object; an intransitive one does not.

words.group: Grammar: verbs that take an object, and verbs that do not
words.childMeaning: Describing a verb that takes no object.
practiceSentences: In "the river rose", "rose" is intransitive.
Is arrive transitive or intransitive?
An intransitive verb is complete without an object.
You cannot make an intransitive verb passive.
Intransitive verbs act without acting on anything.

words.group: Grammar: verbs that take an object, and verbs that do not
words.childMeaning: An -ing form of a verb used as a noun.
practiceSentences: In "walking is cheap", the gerund is "walking".
Which gerund is the subject here?
A gerund looks like a verb and behaves like a noun.
She listed swimming, climbing and reading as gerunds.
A gerund names the activity; a participle describes something.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To manage or give out something officially.
practiceSentences: A nurse will administer the medicine.
Who will administer the fund?
The school administers the test every June.
She was chosen to administer the club's money.
It takes two people to administer the survey fairly.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To speak up publicly in support of something.
practiceSentences: She will advocate for a longer lunch break.
Why advocate a rule that costs you something?
A patient speaker will advocate more effectively than an angry one.
They advocate planting trees along every new road.
I advocate starting small and letting success spread.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To give something to someone for a specific purpose.
practiceSentences: The station decided to allocate more airtime to local stories after listeners complained.
How should the council allocate its small technology budget between laptops and internet upgrades?
"We will allocate five minutes per speaker," announced the moderator, "and the timer is merciless."
I allocate the first hour after school to homework, otherwise my evenings dissolve into videos.
The judges allocate points for accuracy, style and teamwork.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To collect information together into one place.
practiceSentences: She will compile the results into one table.
How long will it take to compile the list?
They compile a report at the end of every term.
He compiled a book of local sayings.
Compile your notes before you begin writing.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To get or obtain something from a source.
practiceSentences: Many English words derive from Latin.
Where does this custom derive from?
Plants derive their energy from sunlight.
She derives real pleasure from careful work.
We can derive the answer from the two measurements.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: Very detailed, complicated, and carefully planned, often with decorative extra touches.
practiceSentences: Imani designed an elaborate mural for the library's new reading corner.
Why did the committee choose such an elaborate plan for a simple festival?
Look at that elaborate costume, Sami!
The wedding included an elaborate ceremony that lasted three full days.
Men perform traditional stick dances, and women prepare elaborate, sweet-scented dishes.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To work out and express an idea or plan carefully.
practiceSentences: Take a moment to formulate your question.
How would you formulate the rule in one line?
They formulated a plan over three meetings.
She formulated her argument before writing.
A good hypothesis is hard to formulate.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To put a plan or decision into action.
practiceSentences: The school will implement the new timetable in May.
Who will implement the changes?
It is easier to agree a rule than to implement it.
They implemented the plan one street at a time.
Implement the simplest version first.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To ask for information about something.
practiceSentences: She stopped to inquire about the bus times.
Where should I inquire about the missing parcel?
He inquired politely and got a full answer.
Inquire before you assume the office is closed.
They inquired into the cause of the delay.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To combine parts so that they work as one.
practiceSentences: Integrate the quotation into your own sentence.
How will you integrate the two lists?
The new pupils integrated quickly into the class.
She integrated the diagrams with the text.
A good report integrates evidence and argument.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To discuss something in order to reach an agreement.
practiceSentences: They will negotiate the price before signing.
Who will negotiate on behalf of the class?
She negotiated an extra week for the project.
To negotiate well you must know what you can give up.
The two villages negotiated over the water.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To control something so that it works properly.
practiceSentences: A thermostat regulates the temperature.
Who regulates the quality of the water?
Laws regulate how deep a well may be dug.
The body regulates its own heat.
Rules regulate the game so it stays fair.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To get something back from where it was left or lost.
practiceSentences: The dog was trained to retrieve the ball.
Can you retrieve the file from the archive?
She retrieved her notes from the bottom of the bag.
Divers retrieved the anchor from the seabed.
It is easier to store a thing than to retrieve it.

words.group: Words: finding out and explaining
words.childMeaning: To copy the way something works, in order to study it.
practiceSentences: The tank simulates conditions on the ocean floor.
How do they simulate zero gravity on Earth?
A model can simulate the flow of a river.
They simulated the launch a hundred times.
You cannot simulate every risk in advance.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The business of keeping, lending and moving people's money.
practiceSentences: Mobile banking reached the village before the road did.
How has banking changed in your grandparents' lifetime?
Banking runs on trust more than on buildings.
She works in banking and explains interest very clearly.
Banking lends out the money it is looking after.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
