words.childMeaning: A basic item that people buy and sell, like food or materials.
practiceSentences: Rice is a vital commodity that traders buy and sell in markets across the world.
Why does the price of a common commodity like wheat affect so many families?
"Clean water is the most precious commodity," the teacher reminded us during the lesson.
I learned that oil is a powerful commodity that shapes the economies of many nations.
A commodity is the same wherever it is sold, which is what sets its price.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: A large company that the law treats as a single body.
practiceSentences: The corporation employs people in nine countries.
Which corporation owns the factory now?
A corporation outlives the people who founded it.
A corporation can be sued in its own name.
A corporation is one company; a co-operative is many owners.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: A business, or the willingness to start something difficult.
practiceSentences: The bakery began as a family enterprise.
What enterprise would you start with a small loan?
An enterprise needs a customer before it needs a logo.
Her enterprise in finding a supplier saved the shop.
Enterprise means the business, and also the nerve to begin it.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: To send goods to another country to be sold there.
practiceSentences: The country exports coffee and imports machinery.
What does this region export?
Exports earn the foreign money a country needs.
They began to export once the port was rebuilt.
An export leaves; an import arrives.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The managing of money, or the money needed for something.
practiceSentences: The council could not find the finance for the bridge.
Who manages the finance for the co-operative?
Finance decides which good ideas actually happen.
She studied finance and returned to advise the village.
To finance something is to pay for it over time.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: To bring goods in from another country to sell.
practiceSentences: They import rice when the harvest is poor.
What does the town import that it once made itself?
Imports fill a gap the country cannot fill itself.
A tax on imports protects local makers and raises prices.
Import in and export out, which is how to remember them.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: To make goods in large amounts, usually with machines.
practiceSentences: The plant manufactures roofing sheets.
What do they manufacture here?
To manufacture is to make many, not to make one.
Manufacturing moved to where the power was cheapest.
Manufacture also means to invent an excuse.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The state of having something that belongs to you.
practiceSentences: Ownership of the class library brings the duty to keep every book safe.
Taking ownership of your mistakes shows real courage and honesty.
Who can prove ownership of the bicycle left outside the library?
"With ownership of a garden plot comes the duty to water it," said Grandad.
Signing the papers gave the school full ownership of the new minibus.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The process of making or creating something.
practiceSentences: The factory improved its production by introducing a faster, smarter assembly line.
How long does the production of a single handmade instrument usually take?
"Our play's production begins next week," the drama teacher announced excitedly.
I helped with the production of the school magazine by designing its bright cover.
Production counts what is made; productivity counts how efficiently.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: One part of a country's economy or activity.
practiceSentences: The farming sector employs most people here.
Which sector is growing fastest?
A country that depends on one sector is fragile.
The public sector is paid for out of taxation.
Sector also means a part of a circle.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The system by which a government collects money from people.
practiceSentences: Taxation pays for the roads and the clinics.
Is taxation fairer when the richest pay a larger share?
Taxation takes from everyone and spends on everyone.
The council explained what taxation pays for in this district.
Taxation is the system; a tax is one charge within it.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: Travelling to new places for fun or to learn about them.
practiceSentences: Tourism brings buses full of visitors to our seaside town.
Tourism gives many families in our town their jobs.
How does tourism help protect the old fort?
"Tourism grows when we keep our beaches clean," said the mayor.
My uncle works in tourism, guiding visitors around the city.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The growing of crops and the raising of animals for food.
practiceSentences: Agriculture depends on rain that arrives on time.
What share of the country works in agriculture?
Agriculture feeds a country before it earns for it.
New methods raised what agriculture could produce from one field.
Agriculture is farming, described from a distance.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The roads, power and water a country needs to work.
practiceSentences: No business grows without infrastructure to reach it.
What infrastructure does this district still lack?
Infrastructure costs a great deal and is noticed only when it fails.
The port is the most valuable infrastructure on the coast.
Infrastructure is what everything else is built on top of.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: An official count of everybody living in a country.
practiceSentences: A census is taken once every ten years.
What does the census ask about?
A census plans the schools a district will need.
The census counted more people than anyone expected.
A census counts everyone; a sample counts a few.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: Large in amount or importance.
practiceSentences: The library received a substantial donation that funded meals for many needy families.
How long would it take to save such a substantial amount from weekly pocket money?
"That's a substantial saving," Sami noted, "if we buy in bulk and share the cost."
I put a substantial part of my earnings aside before spending anything on myself.
Substantial means large enough to matter, not merely large.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: Giving a benefit or putting you in a better position.
practiceSentences: Buying together proved advantageous for every stallholder.
Is an early payment advantageous to the seller?
An advantageous deal for one side is rarely lasting.
The position by the road was advantageous for trade.
Advantageous is the adjective of advantage.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: Relying on something or someone else.
practiceSentences: The harvest is dependent on the March rains.
Is the whole plan dependent on one supplier?
A town dependent on a single crop has no cushion.
She was financially dependent until the shop broke even.
Dependent with an e is the adjective; a dependant is a person.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The ability or qualities someone has that could develop into future success.
practiceSentences: Teacher Yasmin always said Imani had real potential as a writer.
Do you think Sami has the potential to lead the debate team?
You have so much potential, Nora, don't let one bad test change that!
The coach saw potential in every player, even the quietest ones.
Solar power has huge potential in a country with so much sunshine.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: Covering everything that is relevant, leaving nothing out.
practiceSentences: The report gave a comprehensive account of every cost.
Is this a comprehensive list or a selection?
A comprehensive answer takes longer and is worth it.
She made a comprehensive survey of every stall in the market.
Comprehensive means complete; comprehensible means understandable.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: Meant to be kept private and shown only to certain people.
practiceSentences: The bank keeps every account confidential.
Which parts of this record are confidential?
Confidential information is lent, not given.
She marked the letter confidential before sending it.
Confidential means private by agreement, not merely secret.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The way something is shared or spread out among a group of people or things.
practiceSentences: Careful distribution meant that the last lorry of rice reached even the most distant village.
The fair distribution of food ensured every family at the gathering was fed.
Why does the uneven distribution of wealth cause problems in so many societies?
Distribution is as difficult as production, and is planned for less.
I helped organise the distribution of books so no classroom was left without any.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: A small amount of something taken to study or test the rest of it.
practiceSentences: A sample is a small part chosen to stand for the whole.
How large a sample would you need to trust the result?
A sample chosen carelessly tells you about nobody.
They tested a sample of grain from every sack.
A census counts everyone; a sample counts a few and reasons from them.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: The value that appears most often in a set of numbers.
practiceSentences: The mode is the price that came up most often.
What is the mode of these market takings?
A set can have two modes, or none at all.
The mode is the only average that works for words as well as numbers.
Mode also means a way of doing something.

words.group: Words: money, trade and how a country earns
words.childMeaning: How probable it is that something will happen.
practiceSentences: The likelihood of rain in March is high.
What is the likelihood of the price falling again?
Likelihood is a judgement, and probability is its number.
They weighed the likelihood of a poor harvest before borrowing.
A small likelihood is not the same as none.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ment
words.childMeaning: A suggestion that is not stated directly but can be understood.
practiceSentences: The implication of the new fitness data was that the squad needed longer recovery periods.
What is the implication for smaller schools if the league raises its entry fees again?
"The implication of your silence," said the captain quietly, "is that you disagree with the plan."
I resented the implication that our team had won only because the referee favoured us.
An implication is carried by a statement; an inference is drawn by a listener.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ment
words.childMeaning: The act of becoming better, or making something better than before.
practiceSentences: Real improvement often comes from small, steady changes rather than one big leap.
Has there been any improvement in her sprint times this season?
The coach measured improvement in seconds, not in effort.
An improvement you cannot measure is a feeling about an improvement.
Improvement plateaus, and the plateau is where most athletes stop.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ment
words.childMeaning: A new method or idea put into practice.
practiceSentences: The clap-skate was an innovation that rewrote the record books.
What innovation changed this sport most?
An innovation is an idea that has actually been used.
Their innovation was a training schedule, not a machine.
An invention is made; an innovation is adopted.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ment
words.childMeaning: The particular way something is understood or explained.
practiceSentences: The referee's interpretation of the rule decided the match.
What interpretation would you offer of this result?
An interpretation is a reading, and other readings exist.
Two officials gave opposite interpretations of the same contact.
An interpretation explains the evidence; the evidence does not explain itself.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: Giving a vaccine so the body can build immunity in advance.
practiceSentences: Vaccination is required before travelling to some tournaments.
Why does vaccination protect people who cannot be vaccinated?
Vaccination trains the immune system without the illness.
The squad completed its vaccination two months before the games.
A vaccine is the substance; vaccination is the act of giving it.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: A graph that plots two measurements against each other.
practiceSentences: A scatter graph shows every athlete as one point.
What does the scatter tell you about the relationship?
A scatter plot reveals a pattern a table hides.
The points scatter widely, so the link is weak.
Scatter also means to throw about, which is what the points seem to do.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: Chosen with no pattern, so every outcome is equally likely.
practiceSentences: A random sample gives everyone the same chance of being picked.
Is that selection random or merely unplanned?
Random does not mean haphazard: it has to be arranged.
Lanes were assigned at random before the heats.
Random means no pattern; arbitrary means no reason.

words.group: Grammar: the three moods a verb can take
words.childMeaning: Describing a verb form used to give an order or instruction.
practiceSentences: Run, jump and throw are all imperatives here.
Which imperative opens the coach's instructions?
An imperative gives an order and often drops its subject.
The signs used the imperative because there was no time to be polite.
An imperative commands; an interrogative asks.

words.group: Grammar: the three moods a verb can take
words.childMeaning: Describing the verb form used to state a fact.
practiceSentences: In "she runs every morning", "runs" is indicative.
Which mood is indicative in this passage?
The indicative states; it does not command or wish.
Almost every sentence you read is in the indicative.
The indicative reports what is; the subjunctive what might be.

words.group: Grammar: the three moods a verb can take
words.childMeaning: Describing the form used to ask a question.
practiceSentences: "Who", "what" and "which" are interrogative words.
Which interrogative would open this question?
An interrogative sentence usually reverses subject and verb.
She rewrote the statement as an interrogative to soften it.
An interrogative asks; an imperative tells.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: A true account of part of the writer's own life.
practiceSentences: Her memoir covers only the year she spent at sea.
How is a memoir different from a biography?
A memoir chooses one thread from a whole life.
He wrote a short memoir of his first job.
A memoir is true, but it is still shaped.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: An article giving the opinion of a newspaper's editor.
practiceSentences: The editorial argued for a safer crossing.
Which editorial did you find most convincing?
An editorial is opinion, not news.
She wrote an editorial for the school paper.
The editorial appears on the same page each week.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: A spoken or written set of remarks that explains or describes an event or work.
practiceSentences: Sami recorded a clear commentary to explain each part of his board.
Why does good commentary describe the action without hiding the facts?
"Keep your commentary calm and precise," Teacher Yasmin coached them.
Maya added a short commentary beside every photograph.
A commentary walks the audience through the evidence step by step.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: A clear explanation or description, often used to introduce a story's characters and setting.
practiceSentences: A novel's exposition should settle the reader into the setting before any trouble begins.
The story's exposition introduces Dina's tailoring shop before the arrival of the mysterious fabric parcel.
How much exposition does a reader need before the conflict over the factory can begin?
"Trim the exposition," suggested Sami, "and reveal the setting gradually through the characters' errands."
I finally understand exposition as the loom on which the rest of the story is woven.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: The style of language a person chooses depending on who they are speaking or writing to.
practiceSentences: Register changes depending on whether you write to a friend or a head teacher.
How would you describe the register of this poster?
Maya switched her register the moment she wrote to the mayor!
Choosing the wrong register can make a letter sound rude by mistake.
A job application and a text message call for a different register.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Describing a question asked to make a point, not to get an answer.
practiceSentences: A rhetorical question does not really expect an answer at all.
Have you ever noticed how often adverts use a rhetorical question?
Leo asked a rhetorical question just to make his point stronger!
The speech opened with a rhetorical question about the empty playground.
A rhetorical question can open an essay strongly.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: A statement or main idea that someone wants to prove in their writing.
practiceSentences: A clear thesis at the start of your essay tells the reader exactly what you will prove.
Maya's thesis argued that mending skills belong on the school curriculum alongside cooking.
Does your thesis about second-hand fashion appear clearly in the opening paragraph?
"State your thesis early," advised the teacher, "then let every paragraph pull in the same direction."
I revised my thesis twice after the research revealed facts I had not expected.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: A note showing where a fact or quotation came from.
practiceSentences: Add a citation for every fact you borrow.
Which citation supports that claim?
A citation names the author and the page.
Without a citation the reader cannot check you.
She missed one citation and had to redo the page.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: The quality of a text whose ideas fit together sensibly.
practiceSentences: The essay lacks coherence between its second and third parts.
What gives a paragraph coherence?
Coherence comes from order, not from long words.
Read it aloud to test its coherence.
Each paragraph added to the coherence of the whole.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Holding together well, with the parts clearly linked.
practiceSentences: A cohesive paragraph reads as one thought.
Is the argument cohesive from start to finish?
Linking words make writing more cohesive.
The team became more cohesive after the trip.
A cohesive text does not make the reader jump.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Arranged in the order that things happened, from earliest to latest.
practiceSentences: The eco-report describes the clothing swap in chronological order, from first poster to final thank-you.
The museum arranged the garments in chronological order, from hand-stitched robes to modern recycled jackets.
Would the documentary work better in chronological order, or should it open with the dramatic ending?
"Present the supply chain in chronological steps," said the teacher, "from cotton seed to shop window."
I organised my design journal in chronological order so I can watch my ideas evolve.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: To say something in a different way, using different words.
practiceSentences: Before you quote the interview, practise how to paraphrase its main argument fairly.
Nora had to paraphrase the scientist's technical report so younger pupils could understand the statistics.
Can you paraphrase the designer's argument without losing the urgency of her original words?
"Do not copy the article," warned the librarian, "paraphrase it and credit the author properly."
I paraphrase difficult paragraphs aloud to myself, which quickly shows me what I misunderstood.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: The particular way one person sees or judges something.
practiceSentences: How does the river look from the fishermen's perspective?
Whose perspective does this chapter take?
"Try seeing the alley from a child's perspective," said Amara.
Interviewing both sides gave the reporters a fresh perspective.
A change of perspective can change the whole argument.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: To combine several ideas or sources into one whole.
practiceSentences: A good conclusion synthesises the evidence.
How will you synthesise three different reports?
She synthesised the interviews into one argument.
To synthesise is more than to summarise.
Synthesise the findings before you judge them.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: To check that something is true or acceptable.
practiceSentences: A second reading will validate the result.
How do you validate a claim you cannot test?
She validated her findings against the records.
Evidence validates an argument; volume does not.
The experiment validated the earlier prediction.

words.group: Words: kinds of writing and how they read
words.childMeaning: Based on ideas rather than on practical experience.
practiceSentences: The plan is theoretical until somebody tries it.
Is this a theoretical or a practical problem?
Theoretical knowledge needs testing in the world.
She gave a theoretical answer, which did not help.
A theoretical risk can still be worth planning for.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: An agreement between groups to work together for a shared purpose.
practiceSentences: The two unions formed an alliance over pay.
What alliance would strengthen this campaign?
An alliance lasts while the shared interest lasts.
The alliance collapsed when one side broke the terms.
An alliance is between equals; an empire is not.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: The sharing of information or ideas between people.
practiceSentences: Poor communication caused the whole delay.
What communication does a team of forty actually need?
Communication is what was understood, not what was said.
The office improved after one change to its communication.
Communication runs both ways or it is an announcement.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: An act that the law forbids and punishes.
practiceSentences: Reporting a crime is the first step to solving it.
What makes an act a crime rather than a mistake?
A crime is defined by law, and laws differ between countries.
The town's crime rate fell after the lighting improved.
A crime harms a person and also the public order.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: The managing of relations between countries by discussion.
practiceSentences: Diplomacy settled the dispute without a shot.
What does diplomacy achieve that force cannot?
Diplomacy works slowly and is noticed only when it fails.
Years of diplomacy produced a single page of agreement.
Diplomacy also means handling people tactfully.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: The state of everyone having the same rights and opportunities.
practiceSentences: Equality before the law means the same rules for everyone.
Is equality of opportunity the same as equality of outcome?
Equality is a starting point, not a result.
The reform aimed at equality of pay for the same work.
Equality treats people the same; equity treats them as needed.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Ideas about right and wrong, and how people should act.
practiceSentences: Medical ethics decide what a doctor may not do.
What ethics should govern a company's advertising?
Ethics ask what is right, not what is allowed.
The council published a code of ethics for its officers.
Ethics is the study; a rule is one of its conclusions.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: The arrival of people to live in a country not their own.
practiceSentences: Immigration has shaped every city on this coast.
How does immigration change a workforce?
Immigration brings skills as well as needs.
The port town grew through a century of immigration.
Immigration is arriving; emigration is leaving.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: An established body with a lasting public purpose.
practiceSentences: A school is an institution, not merely a building.
Which institution decides this?
An institution outlives the people who run it.
Trust in an institution is slow to build and quick to lose.
An institution can also be a long-standing custom.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Laws, considered together, or the making of them.
practiceSentences: New legislation raised the minimum working age.
What legislation covers this kind of work?
Legislation is written by a parliament and applied by a court.
The legislation took three years to pass.
Legislation is the law; enforcement is another matter.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: The work a person does to earn a living.
practiceSentences: The census records each adult's occupation.
What occupation would suit you?
An occupation is what you do; a career is where it goes.
Her occupation changed three times in twenty years.
Occupation also means holding a place by force.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: To make changes to something in order to improve it.
practiceSentences: The council promised to reform the unfair rules that had troubled the community for years.
Why is it sometimes difficult to reform a system that many people are used to?
"We must reform these laws," the leader argued, "to protect the rights of everyone."
I signed a petition urging the school to reform its outdated recycling policy.
To reform is to reshape what exists, not to replace it.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: A person forced to leave their home country or region because of danger, war or disaster.
practiceSentences: They arrived at a refugee camp exhausted but alive after their long journey.
How many refugee families reached the camp in that same difficult month?
What courage it must take to become a refugee overnight, Jamal thought quietly.
Ayeeyo never forgot the kindness shown to her family in the refugee camp.
The new refugee students learned the language with astonishing speed.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: A formal written agreement between countries.
practiceSentences: The treaty ended forty years of dispute.
Which countries signed the treaty?
A treaty binds the country, not the government that signed it.
The treaty set the border along the river.
A treaty is written down; an understanding may not be.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: All the people who work for an employer or in a country.
practiceSentences: The factory's workforce doubled in two years.
How large is the workforce in this district?
A skilled workforce attracts the businesses that need it.
Half the workforce is under thirty.
Workforce counts the people; labour counts the work.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: The judges and courts of a country, taken together.
practiceSentences: The judiciary applies the law that parliament writes.
Why must the judiciary stay independent of government?
An independent judiciary can rule against the state.
The judiciary interprets legislation case by case.
The judiciary judges; the legislature legislates.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: A town or district with its own local government.
practiceSentences: The municipality collects the waste and lights the streets.
Which municipality does this street belong to?
A municipality raises some of its own money.
The municipality decided to rebuild the market.
A municipality is local government with a boundary.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Being responsible for your actions and ready to explain or answer for them.
practiceSentences: Sir explained that they had added the duty to teach accountability.
Why does accountability matter more to adults than to students, Sir?
Real accountability means admitting a mistake, not just following orders!
Zara argued that accountability should apply to teachers as well as students.
Publishing the accounts online improves accountability.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Being honest and having strong moral principles, even when no one is watching.
practiceSentences: The accountant's integrity was tested when her manager asked her to hide the missing money.
Why is integrity more valuable in a leader than charisma or clever speeches?
"Integrity means doing right when nobody is watching," Teacher Yasmin reminded us before the unsupervised test.
I showed integrity by admitting the broken microscope was my fault, even though no one had seen.
His campaign slogan was simple: Integrity is action.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: The settling of a dispute with the help of a neutral person.
practiceSentences: Mediation settled the argument before it reached a court.
When is mediation better than a ruling?
Mediation works only if both sides agree to it.
The two departments accepted mediation and reached terms.
Mediation helps two sides agree; a judgement decides for them.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Discussion aimed at reaching an agreement.
practiceSentences: The negotiation lasted eleven hours.
What does each side want from this negotiation?
Negotiation needs something each side is willing to give.
After a long negotiation both sides claimed a victory.
Negotiation is talking towards a deal, not away from one.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Collaboration is the act of working together with other people to reach a shared goal.
practiceSentences: Without collaboration, the tree-planting programme would never have reached so many villages.
Could better collaboration between schools help clean up more of the river each year?
What excellent collaboration the eco-club showed during the survey, Teacher Yasmin said!
Amal believed collaboration mattered more than any single person's effort.
The mural was a collaboration between three schools.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Permission that someone gives to allow something to happen.
practiceSentences: You must obtain your parents' consent before signing up for the after-school job scheme.
Why is consent so important before a company uses someone's photograph in an advertisement?
"I give my consent," Dad wrote, "for Amara to join the community work experience."
I would never share a friend's story without first asking for their consent.
Consent must be freely given, or it is not consent at all.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Taking part in something along with other people.
practiceSentences: Participation in the survey was higher than expected.
What raises participation in a local election?
Participation is not the same as agreement.
The scheme depends on the participation of every household.
Participation means taking part, not merely being present.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Speaking or arguing publicly in support of a cause.
practiceSentences: Her advocacy changed the council's mind in a year.
What advocacy would help this campaign most?
Advocacy is patient work with very few quick victories.
The group's advocacy won safer crossings for the school.
Advocacy speaks for a cause; mediation speaks for neither side.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: Treating all sides fairly, without favouring any.
practiceSentences: A referee's impartiality is the whole basis of the game.
How is impartiality shown rather than claimed?
Impartiality means having no stake in the outcome.
The inquiry was praised for its impartiality.
Impartiality is not indifference; it is fairness under pressure.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ivity
words.childMeaning: A careful search made to find out the true facts about something.
practiceSentences: The investigation took four months and changed one paragraph of the report.
What investigation would settle the question?
An investigation follows the evidence rather than the suspicion.
She opened an investigation into how the post was advertised.
An investigation looks for facts; an inquiry may look for blame.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ivity
words.childMeaning: Something that restricts what can be done or known.
practiceSentences: Every method has a limitation, and honest work names it.
What is the main limitation of this study?
A limitation stated is a limitation half answered.
Her only limitation was the time she could give it.
A limitation restricts; a weakness undermines.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ivity
words.childMeaning: The quality of being new and not copied from anything.
practiceSentences: Originality is rarer than the word suggests.
What gives this proposal its originality?
Originality is not the same as never having been influenced.
The judges rewarded originality over polish.
Originality is being first; creativity is being able to be.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -ity and -ivity
words.childMeaning: How much is produced for the effort or time put in.
practiceSentences: Productivity rose when the shifts were shortened.
How would you measure productivity in this job?
Productivity counts output against input, and both need defining.
Long hours and high productivity are not the same thing.
Productivity is a ratio; production is a total.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: The state of wanting paid work and not having it.
practiceSentences: Unemployment among school leavers rose for a third year.
What causes unemployment in a town with one industry?
Unemployment counts those looking for work, not everyone without it.
The figures hid unemployment behind part-time contracts.
Unemployment is measured; the experience of it is not.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: To place things in order according to their value or size.
practiceSentences: Rank these five options before you argue for any of them.
How would you rank the candidates on evidence alone?
Ranking forces a choice that listing avoids.
She ranked the tasks and the timetable wrote itself.
To rank is to order; to rate is to score each one separately.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: To present an idea in a way that shapes how it is understood.
practiceSentences: How you frame the question decides which answers are possible.
Would you frame this as a cost or as an investment?
To frame an argument is to choose what it is about before arguing it.
She framed the delay as a chance to test the design again.
Frame also means the structure that holds something up.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: To consider the importance of things against each other.
practiceSentences: Weigh the cost of training against the years it buys you.
How do you weigh a certain small gain against an uncertain large one?
To weigh two options is to admit both have something in them.
She weighed the offer carefully and turned it down.
Weigh also means to measure how heavy something is.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: To say or write something again in different words.
practiceSentences: Rephrase the question if nobody answers it.
How would you rephrase this for a younger reader?
Rephrasing something you half understand shows you which half.
She rephrased the offer and it suddenly sounded fair.
To rephrase is to change the words; to paraphrase is to compress them too.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: To protect something or someone from criticism, attack or harm.
practiceSentences: Be ready to defend every figure in the proposal.
How would you defend this decision to somebody who disagrees?
To defend a claim is to give the reasons, not to repeat it louder.
Imani defended her conclusion without once raising her voice.
A claim you cannot defend is a claim you should not have made.

words.group: Grammar: sentences that exclaim, and words that join equals
words.childMeaning: Describing a sentence that expresses strong feeling.
practiceSentences: What a difference a year makes is an exclamatory sentence.
Which exclamatory sentence would suit this ending?
An exclamatory sentence ends with an exclamation mark.
She cut every exclamatory sentence from the formal letter.
An exclamatory sentence exclaims; a declarative one states.

words.group: Grammar: sentences that exclaim, and words that join equals
words.childMeaning: Describing a word that joins two parts of equal weight.
practiceSentences: "And", "but" and "or" are coordinating conjunctions.
Which coordinating conjunction fits this sentence?
A coordinating conjunction joins equals; neither clause depends on the other.
She used a coordinating conjunction where a full stop would have been stronger.
Coordinating joins equals; subordinating makes one depend on the other.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A chart of bars showing how often values fall in each range.
practiceSentences: The histogram shows how many pupils scored in each band.
What does this histogram tell you about the class?
A histogram has no gaps between its bars.
She drew a histogram of the daily rainfall.
A histogram groups values; a bar chart names them.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A whole number, with no fraction or decimal part.
practiceSentences: Seven is an integer; seven and a half is not.
Which of these values is an integer?
Integers include negative whole numbers too.
Round the answer to the nearest integer.
Zero is an integer, and it is neither positive nor negative.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: The answer you get when you divide one number by another.
practiceSentences: Twenty divided by four gives a quotient of five.
What is the quotient in this division?
The quotient may have a remainder beside it.
Write the quotient above the division line.
A larger divisor makes a smaller quotient.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: An angle larger than a right angle but less than a straight one.
practiceSentences: An obtuse angle is more than ninety degrees.
Is this angle obtuse or reflex?
A triangle can have only one obtuse angle.
The two roads met at an obtuse angle.
Obtuse angles look open rather than sharp.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: At a right angle to something else.
practiceSentences: The post stands perpendicular to the ground.
Which line is perpendicular to this one?
Perpendicular lines cross at ninety degrees.
She checked the wall was perpendicular with a square.
Perpendicular and parallel are opposites here.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A line on a map running from the North Pole to the South.
practiceSentences: The prime meridian passes through Greenwich.
Which meridian runs closest to your town?
Every meridian is a line of longitude.
Meridians meet at both poles.
Time zones are measured from the prime meridian.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: A number with more than two factors.
practiceSentences: Nine is a composite number.
Which of these numbers is composite?
Every whole number above one is prime or composite.
A composite number can be broken into factors.
Four is the smallest composite number.

words.group: Words: number, shape and data
words.childMeaning: The number being divided.
practiceSentences: In twenty divided by five, twenty is the dividend.
What is the dividend in this calculation?
The dividend sits inside the division sign.
Divide the dividend by the divisor.
A larger dividend gives a larger quotient.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A material that lets heat or electricity pass through it.
practiceSentences: Copper is an excellent conductor of electricity.
Which metal is the better conductor?
A conductor lets energy through; an insulator does not.
Water is a conductor, which is why wet hands are dangerous.
A conductor also leads an orchestra or takes fares on a bus.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: Happening or existing right now, in the present.
practiceSentences: The current issue of The Beacon covers the qualifying trials in detail.
Is the current head teacher the same one who taught Amara's parents?
Rohan, please check the current deadline before you submit anything!
Sana's current training plan is far tougher than last year's.
Keep your contact details current in case the school must reach you.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A material that stops heat or electricity passing through.
practiceSentences: Rubber is an insulator, which is why cables are coated.
Which insulator would keep the water hottest?
An insulator traps air, and trapped air does the work.
Wool is a good insulator even when it is thin.
An insulator blocks; a conductor lets through.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: To do with heat.
practiceSentences: Thermal energy moves from hot to cold, always.
What thermal protection does the roof need?
A thermal image shows where a building leaks heat.
Birds ride a thermal to gain height without flapping.
Thermal comes from the Greek word for heat.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: The distance between one wave's peak and the next.
practiceSentences: Red light has a longer wavelength than blue.
What wavelength does this station broadcast on?
A shorter wavelength carries more energy.
The wavelength of a sea wave can be measured from a pier.
Being on the same wavelength means understanding each other.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: The height of a wave from its middle to its peak.
practiceSentences: A louder sound has a greater amplitude.
How does amplitude differ from wavelength?
Amplitude measures the size of a wave, not its spacing.
The amplitude fell as the ripples spread outwards.
Amplitude is how big; frequency is how often.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: To do with the huge plates that make up the Earth's surface.
practiceSentences: Tectonic plates move a few centimetres each year.
Which tectonic boundary runs beneath this valley?
Tectonic movement built every mountain range on Earth.
An earthquake happens where two tectonic plates slip.
A tectonic shift also means a very large change in anything.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: How steeply a line or a slope rises or falls.
practiceSentences: The road's gradient is one in ten.
What is the gradient of this line?
A gradient of zero is flat.
The river slows where the gradient eases.
Gradient is the rise divided by the distance across.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A pair of numbers giving an exact position on a grid.
practiceSentences: The coordinates place the well at the field's corner.
What are the coordinates of this point?
Coordinates name one spot and no other.
She read the coordinates from the map's edges.
Coordinates go across first, then up.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A curved part of the edge of a circle.
practiceSentences: The compass drew a neat arc across the page.
How long is this arc?
An arc is part of a circle's circumference.
The ball travelled in a high arc over the wall.
An arc is curved; a chord is the straight line across it.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A straight line that touches a curve at exactly one point.
practiceSentences: The tangent touches the circle and does not cross it.
Where does the tangent meet the curve?
A tangent meets a circle at one point only.
She drew a tangent to find the slope at that instant.
To go off on a tangent is to leave the subject suddenly.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: To cross over or meet at a point.
practiceSentences: The two roads intersect beside the market.
Where do these lines intersect?
Two straight lines intersect once, or never.
The circles intersect at two points.
To intersect is to cross; to bisect is to cut in half.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: To cut something into two equal parts.
practiceSentences: The line bisects the angle exactly.
Which line bisects this shape?
To bisect is to halve, not merely to divide.
A diagonal bisects a square into two triangles.
Bisect means cut in two; trisect means cut in three.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: Exactly the same in shape and size.
practiceSentences: The two triangles are congruent.
Are these shapes congruent or merely similar?
Congruent shapes match exactly when one is placed on the other.
Turning a shape does not stop it being congruent.
Congruent means identical; similar means the same shape at a different size.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A flat shape with four straight sides.
practiceSentences: A square is one kind of quadrilateral.
Which quadrilateral has no parallel sides?
Every quadrilateral's angles add up to 360 degrees.
She sorted each quadrilateral by its parallel sides.
A quadrilateral takes its name from quad, four, and lateral, side.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel.
practiceSentences: A parallelogram leans, but its opposite sides stay parallel.
Is a rectangle a parallelogram?
A parallelogram's opposite angles are equal.
She pushed the square sideways into a parallelogram.
Every rectangle is a parallelogram; not every parallelogram is a rectangle.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A parallelogram with all four sides the same length.
practiceSentences: A rhombus is a pushed-over square.
Is this shape a rhombus or a kite?
A rhombus has four equal sides and no right angles needed.
The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles.
A square is a rhombus that also has right angles.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides.
practiceSentences: A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides.
Which side of this trapezium is the longer parallel one?
A trapezium's area uses the average of the two parallel sides.
The dam's cross-section is a trapezium.
In British usage a trapezium has one parallel pair.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A solid shape with the same cross-section all the way along.
practiceSentences: A tin of beans is a circular prism.
What shape is this prism's cross-section?
Every prism keeps the same shape from end to end.
A glass prism splits white light into a spectrum.
Two identical ends make a prism; one point makes a pyramid.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A solid shape whose sides meet at a single point above its base.
practiceSentences: A pyramid narrows to one point at the top.
How many faces does this pyramid have?
A pyramid can have any polygon as its base.
The tent was pitched in the shape of a pyramid.
A pyramid rises to a point; a prism does not.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: Shaped like a triangle, or having three sides.
practiceSentences: The roof panel is triangular.
Which triangular shape is the strongest?
A triangular frame does not fold the way a square one does.
She cut the cloth into triangular pieces.
Triangular describes the shape; a triangle is the shape itself.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: Sliding a shape to a new position without turning or resizing it.
practiceSentences: A translation slides the shape without turning it.
How far is this translation, and in which direction?
A translation changes position and nothing else.
She described the translation as three right and two up.
Translation also means putting words into another language.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: To do with turning around a fixed point.
practiceSentences: The shape has rotational symmetry of order four.
Does this pattern have rotational symmetry?
Rotational symmetry means it looks the same after a turn.
A wheel's rotational movement is what carries the cart.
Rotational is turning; translational is sliding.

words.group: Words: forces, shapes and measuring the Earth
words.childMeaning: A pattern of shapes that fits together with no gaps.
practiceSentences: The floor tiles form a perfect tessellation.
Which shapes make a tessellation on their own?
A tessellation leaves no gaps and no overlaps.
A hexagon tessellation is why a honeycomb is strong.
A circle cannot make a tessellation, however it is arranged.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ition
words.childMeaning: A skill, quality, or certificate that makes someone suitable for a job.
practiceSentences: A recognised qualification in accounting opened doors that years of unrecorded experience could not.
Which qualification would help most if you wanted to work as a wildlife photographer?
"Experience matters," said the recruiter, "but without the right qualification your application stops at the first desk."
I plan to earn a lifeguarding qualification next summer so I can work at the community pool.
A qualification is also a limit added to a claim, as in a qualified apology.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ition
words.childMeaning: The act of knowing something again, or of publicly acknowledging it.
practiceSentences: Face recognition unlocks the phone in less than a second.
What recognition did the reporters receive for the investigation?
Recognition of a pattern is faster than reasoning about it.
The paper won recognition it had not sought.
Recognition can mean identifying something, or honouring somebody.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ition
words.childMeaning: The way something or someone is shown or described.
practiceSentences: The film's representation of the town annoyed everyone who lives there.
What representation of young people does this article offer?
A representation is always a choice about what to leave out.
The mural was a colourful representation of the many cultures within our school.
Representation also means speaking or acting on behalf of others.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: An image or figure standing for a person online.
practiceSentences: Her avatar is a drawing of a heron.
What does your choice of avatar tell a stranger?
An avatar hides a face and reveals a preference.
The forum required an avatar and a name that was not your own.
An avatar represents you; it is not a portrait of you.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A machine's ability to perform tasks that would need human thought.
practiceSentences: Artificial intelligence now writes the first draft of some news reports.
What tasks does this intelligence actually perform?
An intelligence that sounds confident is not thereby correct.
Intelligence also means information gathered about an opponent.
Human intelligence and machine intelligence are not the same thing.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A method by which a computer improves from data rather than from instructions.
practiceSentences: Machine learning finds patterns nobody wrote down.
What data was this learning system trained on?
A learning system repeats whatever bias its data contained.
The recommendations improved as the learning continued.
Learning also means what you do when you find out something new.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Unfairly favouring one side over another.
practiceSentences: The report was biased in what it left out, not in what it said.
Is this source biased, and does it declare it?
A biased account can contain nothing but true statements.
She read two biased papers to find the shape of the argument.
Biased leans one way; balanced gives each side its best case.

words.group: Grammar: words that join unequals, and pairs that work together
words.childMeaning: Describing a word that makes one clause depend on another.
practiceSentences: "Because", "although" and "unless" are subordinating conjunctions.
Which subordinating conjunction fits this sentence?
A subordinating conjunction turns a clause into a part of another.
Journalists use subordinating clauses to bury what they would rather not stress.
Subordinating makes one clause depend; coordinating joins equals.

words.group: Grammar: words that join unequals, and pairs that work together
words.childMeaning: Describing a pair of words that work together in a sentence.
practiceSentences: "Either" and "or" are correlative conjunctions.
Which correlative pair would suit this sentence?
A correlative pair must match: neither goes with nor.
She used the correlative pair not only and but also in one sentence.
Correlative conjunctions come in pairs; coordinating ones stand alone.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: A person who manages and organises the daily running of an institution such as a school.
practiceSentences: The administrator confirmed that no such closure letter had ever existed.
Has the administrator seen the video that is worrying so many students?
Ask the administrator yourself, Rohan suggested, she will know the truth!
A calm conversation with the administrator ended the whole rumour within minutes.
First, they visited the school office and asked the administrator directly.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: A person who receives help, money or an advantage.
practiceSentences: The village was the main beneficiary of the grant.
Who is the beneficiary of this scheme?
A beneficiary need not have asked for anything.
She named her sister as the beneficiary.
Every beneficiary was written to in advance.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: A person or firm hired to do a particular job.
practiceSentences: The contractor begins work on the roof in June.
Which contractor won the bid?
A contractor is paid for the job, not the hours.
The contractor left the site tidy each evening.
They asked three contractors for a price.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: A person elected to serve on a local council.
practiceSentences: The councillor visited the flooded street herself.
Which councillor represents this ward?
A councillor is elected by local people.
She wrote to her councillor about the bus route.
The councillor voted against the proposal.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: The person in a court case who is accused.
practiceSentences: The defendant listened without speaking.
What did the defendant say in reply?
A defendant is innocent until it is proved otherwise.
The defendant was represented by a lawyer.
Both the defendant and the witness were questioned.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: A person chosen to represent others; to give a task to someone.
practiceSentences: A wise editor learns to delegate research tasks instead of exhausting herself before every deadline.
Whom will the committee choose as its delegate for the national youth media conference?
"I delegate the interviews to you two," said Sami, "while I chase the missing statistics."
Being chosen as our class delegate taught me to present opinions that were not always my own.
Each district sends one delegate to the youth parliament.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: A person who puts money into something to earn more later.
practiceSentences: An investor paid for the new machinery.
What does an investor expect in return?
Every investor accepts some risk.
The investor asked to see the accounts first.
A patient investor waits years for a return.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: A person who pays taxes to the government.
practiceSentences: Every taxpayer helps fund the schools.
What does the taxpayer get in return?
A taxpayer has a right to ask how money is spent.
The road was built with taxpayers' money.
Taxpayers were asked for their views first.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: A person who pays to live in a house or flat.
practiceSentences: The tenant upstairs waters the plants on the shared balcony.
The new tenant moved into the flat above the bakery.
Does the tenant help water the shared garden too?
"A good tenant keeps the house tidy," said the landlord.
My uncle is a tenant in a building near the library.

words.group: Words: government, work and money
words.childMeaning: The buying and selling of goods on a large scale.
practiceSentences: The port has been a centre of commerce for centuries.
How has commerce changed the town?
Commerce needs roads as much as it needs money.
Online commerce reached the village late.
Commerce and trade mean much the same thing.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: How much data a connection can carry in a given time.
practiceSentences: Video uses far more bandwidth than text.
How much bandwidth does the school have?
Bandwidth is shared, so everyone slows down together.
Low bandwidth is why the picture keeps freezing.
Bandwidth also means how much attention a person can spare.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: A small file a website stores on your device to remember you.
practiceSentences: A cookie remembers that you are already signed in.
Why does this site ask about cookies?
A cookie can also record which pages you visited.
She cleared the cookies and had to sign in again.
A cookie is a file, not the biscuit.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: A law that protects someone’s creative work so that others cannot use it without permission.
practiceSentences: The author holds the copyright, so nobody may reprint her book without permission.
Why does copyright matter to musicians who depend on their songs for an income?
Copyright expires, and the work then belongs to everyone.
Copyright protects the expression, not the idea behind it.
I learned that copyright protects artists so others cannot steal their creative ideas.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: Using messages or posts online to hurt or frighten somebody.
practiceSentences: Cyberbullying follows a person home, which is what makes it different.
What should you do if you witness cyberbullying?
Cyberbullying leaves a record, and that record can help.
The school's policy treats cyberbullying as seriously as any bullying.
Cyberbullying is not an argument; it is repeated and one-sided.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: A collection of related information gathered for study.
practiceSentences: The dataset holds ten years of rainfall readings.
How large is this dataset?
A dataset is only as good as how it was collected.
She cleaned the dataset before drawing any chart.
A dataset can be honest and still be misleading.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: The name that identifies a website, or an area of knowledge.
practiceSentences: The school registered its own domain last year.
Which domain does this address belong to?
A domain name points to a computer somewhere.
Ancient history is not her domain.
A domain ending in .org tells you very little by itself.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: A system that blocks unwanted traffic reaching a network.
practiceSentences: The firewall blocked the connection before it reached us.
What does the firewall let through?
A firewall filters traffic; it does not remove a virus already inside.
The school's firewall blocks some sites the class needs.
A firewall was originally a real wall that stopped a fire spreading.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: Pictures and designs produced on a computer.
practiceSentences: The graphics carry more of the argument than the text does.
What graphics would make this data clearer?
Good graphics answer a question; decoration does not.
She redrew the graphics so they worked in black and white.
Graphics takes a plural verb even for one image set.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: One of the tiny dots that together make a screen image.
practiceSentences: Zoom in far enough and you see every pixel.
How many pixels does this screen have?
A pixel holds one colour and nothing else.
More pixels mean a sharper picture and a larger file.
Pixel is short for picture element.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: A talk given with slides or images to explain something.
practiceSentences: Her presentation used six slides and no notes.
How long should the presentation last?
A presentation is judged on what the audience takes away.
He rehearsed the presentation until the timing was right.
Presentation also means the way something is arranged for viewing.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: Playing video or music over the internet as it arrives, without downloading it first.
practiceSentences: Streaming plays the film as it arrives, so nothing is stored.
Why does streaming need more bandwidth than downloading a page?
Streaming stops the moment the connection does.
The match was watched by streaming in four countries at once.
Streaming also describes water flowing steadily, which is where the word came from.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: The trace a person or activity leaves behind.
practiceSentences: Everything you post adds to your digital footprint.
How large is this factory's carbon footprint?
A footprint is left whether you meant to leave it or not.
She checked her own footprint by searching her name.
A footprint is also the mark a shoe leaves in soft ground.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: An unfair preference or opinion that affects how you think or act.
practiceSentences: A good sports journalist checks every report carefully to remove any hint of bias.
Did the judges show bias towards the home gymnast, or was her routine simply better?
"Commentators must set aside personal bias," explained the editor, "or viewers will stop trusting the coverage."
I noticed my own bias when I cheered a foul simply because it helped my team.
She explained how bias grows in silence.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: To say that something is true, or to ask for something you believe is yours.
practiceSentences: The advert's claim that the phone battery lasts three days collapsed under the reviewers' testing.
Should a newspaper publish a dramatic claim before its reporters have verified the facts?
"Anyone can claim anything online," warned the librarian, "so always trace the original source."
I doubted the influencer's claim about the miracle study app, so I tested it myself for a week.
First, who is making this claim, and are they named?

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: The quality of a text whose parts hold together.
practiceSentences: Linking words give a paragraph its cohesion.
What gives this article its cohesion?
Cohesion is how it holds together; coherence is whether it makes sense.
The draft lost its cohesion when two paragraphs were swapped.
Cohesion can be added; coherence has to be thought.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: Passing off someone else's work as your own.
practiceSentences: A citation is what stands between quoting and plagiarism.
How does a citation prevent plagiarism?
Plagiarism is not avoided by changing a few words.
The essay was returned unmarked because of plagiarism.
Plagiarism steals the credit, not only the words.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: The combining of several sources or ideas into one whole.
practiceSentences: A good conclusion is a synthesis, not a summary.
What synthesis do these three reports allow?
Synthesis puts sources into conversation with each other.
Her synthesis of the interviews produced one clear argument.
A summary shortens one source; a synthesis joins several.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: Depending on another part, as a subordinate clause depends on a main one.
practiceSentences: A subordinate clause cannot stand as a sentence on its own.
Which part of this sentence is subordinate?
A subordinate clause usually opens with a word like although or because.
She joined the two ideas with a subordinate clause.
Subordinate also describes a person of lower rank.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: Describing a verb, such as should or must, that shows how certain or necessary something is.
practiceSentences: The word "might" is a modal verb that softens a claim.
Which modal verb would make this less certain?
A modal verb shows how sure or how necessary something is.
Advertising prefers the modal verbs must and should to might and could.
Modal verbs never take an -s in the third person.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: A note added to a text to explain or comment on it.
practiceSentences: Her annotation explained why the figure was doubtful.
What annotation would help a reader here?
An annotation belongs beside the claim it questions.
The margin was full of annotations by the second reading.
An annotation comments; a citation credits.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: An answer that argues against a point somebody has made.
practiceSentences: Her rebuttal took the strongest objection first.
What rebuttal would you offer to that claim?
A rebuttal must answer the argument, not the person.
The editorial printed a rebuttal the following week.
A rebuttal disagrees with reasons; a denial simply disagrees.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: A statement an argument assumes to be true and builds on.
practiceSentences: The whole argument rests on one unstated premise.
What premise is this article assuming?
A false premise ruins a perfectly logical argument.
She questioned the premise rather than the conclusion.
A premise is where an argument starts, not where it ends.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: A strong statement that something is true.
practiceSentences: Support every assertion in your report with a fact, a figure, or a named source.
The article's boldest assertion, that repairing clothes could halve textile waste, demanded strong supporting data.
What evidence would support the assertion that school uniforms reduce pressure on poorer families?
"That assertion needs a source," noted the editor, circling the sentence about water usage.
I have learnt to treat every confident assertion in advertising as a question needing proof.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: A change from one state or stage to another.
practiceSentences: The transition from print to screen took twenty years.
What manages the transition between these two paragraphs?
A transition should carry the reader, not jolt them.
The film's transition to the next scene is deliberately abrupt.
A transition is the moving between; a change is the result.

words.group: Words: media, argument and what to believe
words.childMeaning: Able to be reached, entered or understood by everyone.
practiceSentences: The site is accessible to readers using a screen reader.
Is this explanation accessible to a younger audience?
An accessible design is not a simplified one.
Captions make a video accessible to more people.
Accessible means everyone can get to it, in every sense.

units.title: The Digital World and Future Innovation

words.group: Word building: -ance, -ation and -ility
words.childMeaning: The importance of something, or how much it matters.
practiceSentences: The significance of the result was clear only after the second trial.
What is the significance of this date in the file?
Significance is not the same as size: a tiny change can matter enormously.
She explained the significance of the missing metadata.
In statistics, significance means a result is unlikely to be chance.

words.group: Word building: -ance, -ation and -ility
words.childMeaning: Concentrating on one narrow area of work or study.
practiceSentences: Her specialisation is the security of medical devices.
What specialisation would you choose in computing?
Specialisation buys depth and costs breadth.
Early specialisation can close doors you have not seen yet.
Specialisation narrows on purpose; a general training does not.

words.group: Word building: -ance, -ation and -ility
words.childMeaning: The quality of staying steady and not changing unexpectedly.
practiceSentences: The system ran for a year without losing stability.
What threatens the stability of this network?
Stability is boring, which is how you know it is working.
They chose stability over the newest version.
Stability resists change; rigidity cannot accept it.

words.group: Grammar: leaving words out, and putting words in their place
words.childMeaning: Leaving out words that the reader can supply from context.
practiceSentences: In "she can code and he cannot", ellipsis removes the second "code".
Where has ellipsis been used in this sentence?
Ellipsis avoids repeating what has just been said.
Speech uses ellipsis constantly without anyone noticing.
Ellipsis also names the three dots that mark an omission.

words.group: Grammar: leaving words out, and putting words in their place
words.childMeaning: Replacing a word or phrase with a shorter one to avoid repeating it.
practiceSentences: In "I have a laptop and she has one too", the substitution is "one".
Which word is doing the substitution here?
Substitution replaces; ellipsis removes altogether.
Careful substitution keeps a paragraph from repeating a long noun.
Words like one, do and so are the commonest substitutions in English.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: A set of steps a computer follows to complete a task.
practiceSentences: A recipe is an algorithm you can eat.
What does this algorithm do first?
An algorithm must work for every case, not one.
The search algorithm ranks the results.
She wrote the algorithm out in plain English first.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: The use of machines to do work people once did.
practiceSentences: Automation changed how the factory was staffed.
What tasks does automation handle best?
Automation removes the dull and repeats the exact.
The mill introduced automation ten years ago.
Automation still needs someone to check it.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: Keeping computers and data safe from attack.
practiceSentences: Cybersecurity begins with a strong password.
Why does cybersecurity matter to a school?
Good cybersecurity assumes someone will try.
She works in cybersecurity for a bank.
Cybersecurity is a habit, not a product.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: To prove that someone or something is genuine.
practiceSentences: A password helps authenticate who you are.
How does the system authenticate a user?
Experts were called in to authenticate the painting.
Two steps authenticate the account more safely.
You must authenticate before the file will open.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: Scrambling information so only the right person can read it.
practiceSentences: Encryption protects the message in transit.
How strong is the encryption on this site?
Encryption turns readable text into nonsense.
Without encryption anyone on the network could read it.
Encryption is old; only the maths is new.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: The part of a system a person actually uses.
practiceSentences: A clear interface needs no instructions.
What is wrong with this interface?
The interface hides the complicated part.
She redesigned the interface for younger users.
A good interface makes the right action obvious.

words.group: Words: computers, data and staying safe
words.childMeaning: Software written to damage or break into a computer.
practiceSentences: Malware often arrives in an attachment.
How did the malware reach the network?
Malware can sit unnoticed for months.
Never open a file that might carry malware.
Good habits stop more malware than any program.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: Writing that mocks something in order to criticise it.
practiceSentences: The cartoon is satire, not simple insult.
What is this satire actually attacking?
Satire uses humour to make a serious point.
The play was banned because its satire was too accurate.
Satire laughs at power; comedy may laugh at anything.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: A joke that plays on two meanings of one word.
practiceSentences: The headline was a pun on the word current.
Can you spot the pun in this title?
A pun needs a word that means two things at once.
Newspapers use a pun to make a dull story memorable.
A pun works on the page more easily than aloud.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: A phrase that puts two opposite ideas side by side.
practiceSentences: A deafening silence is an oxymoron.
Which oxymoron opens this poem?
An oxymoron contradicts itself on purpose.
The poet used an oxymoron to catch the reader's attention.
An oxymoron is a contradiction that means something.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: The plain dictionary meaning of a word.
practiceSentences: The denotation of home is the place where you live.
What is the denotation of this word?
Denotation is what the dictionary says; connotation is what it suggests.
Two words can share a denotation and feel quite different.
Denotation is fixed; connotation shifts with time and place.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: The feelings or ideas that a word makes you think of, beyond its basic meaning.
practiceSentences: Advertisers know the connotation of the word new, so they print it in bold letters.
Marketers choose 'vintage' over 'used' because its connotation suggests charm rather than wear.
What connotation does the phrase 'fast fashion' carry now that shoppers know its true cost?
"Consider the connotation of 'cheap'," warned the editor, "it can insult the very customers you want."
I realise the connotation of a colour can differ between cultures, which matters in global advertising.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: Describing words chosen to make readers feel strong emotions.
practiceSentences: The appeal used emotive language throughout.
Which emotive word is doing the most work here?
Emotive writing moves a reader before it convinces them.
She replaced the emotive words with plain ones and the case grew stronger.
Emotive is not the same as dishonest, but it is worth noticing.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: A film or programme about real people and real events.
practiceSentences: Unlike a drama, a documentary does not invent characters.
What makes a documentary trustworthy?
A documentary tells a true story about real people and places.
The documentary followed one family for three years.
A documentary still chooses what to show, which is a kind of argument.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: A book that collects original documents on one subject.
practiceSentences: The sourcebook prints the letters in full.
Which sourcebook covers this period?
A sourcebook gives you the evidence rather than the conclusion.
She quoted from the sourcebook rather than the textbook.
A sourcebook collects sources; a textbook explains them.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: A written copy of the exact words spoken in a conversation, interview, or speech.
practiceSentences: Maya highlighted her favourite lines in the interview transcript.
Did you read the whole transcript before answering the questions?
This transcript is fascinating, Sami, Amara explains everything so clearly!
A transcript lets you study exactly what was said, word for word.
The court keeps a transcript of everything said at the trial.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: To do with study and learning, especially at a high level.
